in writing. ‒ the idea is a priori tempting: to tackle unemployment by linking the whole of the supply of and demand for jobs at european level. it does not, however, stand up to scrutiny. the rapporteur notes and regrets in the explanatory statement that the rate of 'mobility' of workers in the union is only 0.29%, a figure which of course does not include posted workers. but he doesn't analyze the fundamentals. how can one reasonably believe that this low rate is due only to a lack of information among potential workers and employers? how can we believe that the lack of appetite of an unemployed frenchman or swede to go to work for 425 euros a month in romania, where that is the average salary, is due only to his ignorance of the job offers available? or that an unemployed romanian is not tempted to make the trip to france, no matter what happens, even if he only finds a job paid for by the smic? your desire to create an artificial single labour market will result in the institutionalisation of social dumping, the threat of subjecting the rights of the unemployed to acceptance of any job, anywhere in europe, and ultimately, a social levelling down. i voted against it.
in writing. ‒ on thursday 25 february, i voted in favour of a text to reform the european employment services network (eures), a european database of jobseekers and job vacancies in europe. to combat unemployment effectively, we must improve the matching of supply and demand in the labour market. with this new eures portal, free and accessible, we will now be able to automatically synchronise cvs with suitable job vacancies. in addition, all vacancies published by public employment offices in the eu member states will be available at european level on the web portal. eures is also a great support tool for frontier workers, who will be able to benefit from essential information on the legislation applicable across borders and will benefit from personalised support in their rights transfer procedures. the member states must now make good use of it!
in writing. ‒ labour market policies are a competence of the member states and the rapporteur, mr becker, has ensured that this prerogative is respected. i do, however, support the idea that the mobility of workers can be encouraged by better european coordination of employment services. that is the whole point of the proposed regulation. the proposal aims to strengthen the eures network by bringing together job vacancies, including traineeships and apprenticeships, and applications for these vacancies under a single label. the public employment services are members of this structure. the provision of these services will be free of charge for applicants and may be chargeable to employers for specific requests. the proposal favours the creation of an instrument for mobility and employment without depriving the member states of their primary competence in the field of employment policy. that is why i supported this text.
in writing. ‒ the original text on the project for a european network of employment services, workers' access to mobility services and further integration of labour markets included the promotion of the single labour and employment market through the eures (european employment services) scheme. it goes without saying that all my colleagues in the enf group opposed this in the committee on employment and social affairs several days ago. the free movement of workers and the linking of job vacancies and jobseekers at european level are a danger for french workers. this system tends to encourage 'brain drain' and thus to widen the gap between southern and eastern europe and northern and western europe. this is therefore in total opposition to the national preference over employment which we have always advocated. i therefore voted against this text.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report by my colleague heinz becker on the european network of employment services (eures), on workers' access to mobility services and on the further integration of labour markets. the aim is to encourage and improve the professional mobility of european workers through the european eures tool. companies can also use it to search for job candidates. in the context of persistent unemployment, especially among young people, which is a priority for my political group, the epp, i support this initiative which aims to boost the european labour market, particularly in border areas, with the possibility of developing partnerships. i welcome the fact that this report was adopted by a large majority.
in writing. ‒ this report is about a commission proposal to improve the eures network. eures is a tool for workers to support them in their professional mobility. it brings together job vacancies from across the union, thus facilitating the mobility of workers within the european union and enabling smes to fill vacancies. at a time of particular difficulty for employment in france and europe, especially for young people, it was obvious to vote in favour of this text which will boost the labour market, particularly in the border areas, while keeping in mind that labour market policies remain the responsibility of the member states.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the report on 'the european network of employment services, workers' access to mobility services and further integration of labour markets' for several reasons. visibility and access to the network remain complex, despite apparent good intentions. the linking of supply and demand at european level poses obvious logistical and resource problems. the system tends to encourage brain drain and thus to widen the gap between southern and eastern europe and northern and western europe. eures ('european employment pole') promotes blackmail on mobility, whereby an unemployed person would not want to work unless he or she is ready to take up an offer elsewhere in europe, wherever it may be, which could potentially pose difficulties with regard to unemployment benefits. this system encourages the uprooting of workers, imposes the single european labour market as the only alternative to unemployment and institutionalizes the precariousness of employment.

in writing. ‒ eures is a cooperation network to facilitate the free movement of workers within the 28 eu member states, switzerland, iceland, liechtenstein and norway. the report before us is intended to make this system more effective. parliament's amendments are aimed at guaranteeing workers' rights. the text thus allows member states to 'refuse or revoke the admission of eures members or partners who violate applicable labour standards and legal requirements, in particular as regards remuneration and working conditions'. it also seeks to combat 'any discrimination based on nationality between workers of the member states in matters of employment, remuneration and other conditions of work and employment within the union'. however, the text takes it as a principle that increasing the mobility of workers is a way of combating unemployment, so i abstained.

in writing. ‒ the establishment of a structured cooperation network allowing all european citizens access to all job vacancies is part of the free movement of workers, a founding pillar of the european union. the measures mentioned are to strengthen cooperation between public employment services, to integrate non-public bodies (trade unions, chambers of commerce), to improve access to the eures portal ('european employment hub') and to create a european coordination portal. this system is dangerous because it further encourages the uprooting of workers, imposes the single european labour market as the only alternative to unemployment and institutionalises the precariousness of employment. in addition, eures promotes the blackmail of mobility, that an unemployed person would not want to work unless he is ready to take up an offer in europe, wherever it may be. we therefore strongly oppose the establishment of this network which will continue to undermine our sovereignty and our economy.

in writing. ‒ as part of the freedoms of movement which are the essence of the european construction, the free movement of workers is essential to any strategy to combat longterm and mass unemployment in an 'optimal monetary area'. by improving the employment prospects of workers and non-workers, and by helping employers to fill their vacancies quickly, mobility ultimately benefits the growth areas of europe. the alarming fact is that the rate of labour mobility in the union is only 0.29% and only 3.1% of european workers are employed in a member state other than their country of origin, despite the fact that there are large disparities in the demand for and supply of jobs between european regions. while labour law is almost exclusively a matter for the member states, this proposal for a regulation aims to strengthen the eures network by improving the information, transparency, accessibility and visibility of a large pool of job vacancies and jobseeker profiles across europe. i voted in favour of this text, which presents a positive outlook for employment, labour mobility and growth in the union.

in writing. ‒ the resolution contains parliament's recommendations to the commission on the recently opened negotiations with tunisia for a 'deep and comprehensive free trade agreement'. while there are some good elements in this text (asymmetry in the agreement, publication of the negotiating mandate, better involvement of civil society, sectoral impact studies), it remains within an economic and neoliberal logic. tunisia occupies a special place in the middle east. the so-called 'arab spring' has been hit hard by terrorists, and everything must be done to ensure that its democratic transition is successful. but while the social question has not been answered, the eu and its member states are only offering it poisoned gifts. after toxic loans that have contributed to the increase of its debt, tunisia should therefore liberalize its economy, sacrifice its traditional agriculture and its environment, all to the benefit of large european companies. i voted against and i am still calling for a real partnership which puts the interests of the people on both sides of the mediterranean above the profits of companies and investors. it is urgent to take account of the real issues in order to give tunisian democracy a chance.

in writing. ‒ this owninitiative parliamentary report, as every year, assesses the functioning of the ecb. it was the subject of more controversy than previous reports to the european parliament in 2014. the report first criticised the negative role played by the ecb in greece and other countries subject to austerity policies. unfortunately, in the final version of the report, these points were removed and the criticism is limited to asking for a thorough assessment of the way the 'troika' operates and of the ecb's participation in the 'troika'. the report also supports the ecb's monetary policy. as i have said in previous years, it is essential to put the ecb under political control. the ecb's activities must be primarily focused on public investment, employment and social cohesion. it is essential to put an end to austerity policies. the ecb must no longer intervene independently in european policies and must act more transparently. we need a european central bank which serves the people, the general interest and not finance. so, not surprisingly, i voted against it.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report to open negotiations on a free trade agreement with australia and new zealand. the text covers a wide range of areas: investment, goods and services, e-commerce, public procurement, state-owned enterprises, energy and plant health barriers, but also agriculture. in this respect, the report recognises the need for safeguard measures such as quotas and transitional periods. however, australian and new zealand farms are very competitive, especially in livestock, milk and cereals. opening free trade negotiations would therefore be dramatic for french livestock and dairy farming. moreover, the preventive measures outlined will certainly only be in place for a time to make way for full free trade. i am deeply opposed to the 'governance of the world economy' to which the text refers, and i cannot support it.
in writing. ‒ due to the high competitiveness of the australian and new zealand agricultural sectors, particularly in livestock, milk and cereals, it is very dangerous to open free trade negotiations with these two countries. this would be the end of the dairy sector and of french livestock. we cannot trust the commission and parliament when they claim to 'preserve' these sensitive sectors. their vision expressed here is to put in place transitional periods, quotas at the beginning, and then to establish aggressive free trade. i therefore opposed this text.

in writing. ‒ on thursday, february 25, i voted in favour of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in attacks on civilians, emergency and medical personnel, ground fighting and shelling in yemen to allow emergency aid to reach the yemeni people. we regret that the humanitarian situation in yemen is deteriorating every day. the conflict in yemen has killed more than 6,100 people, nearly half of them civilians, and wounded about 30,000, according to the un. the european union is not a party to the peace process, but it is a party to the peace process. the european parliament also called for an embargo on arms supplies to saudi arabia, criticising its air strikes and the naval blockade of yemen, which have killed thousands of people.
in writing. in yemen, 6,000 people, including 3,000 civilians, have been killed in a conflict that is in clear violation of international law. in the face of this unacceptable situation, i supported this resolution to call for a ceasefire that allows humanitarian access to the yemeni people and to ask the eu to impose an arms embargo on saudi arabia, the country that leads the arab-sunni coalition which has been shelling the population in its schools, hospitals and aid centres since march 2015. my support for this embargo is in line with the union's 2008 common position on arms exports. this decision requires member states, when exporting arms, to take into account the country of destination's compliance with international humanitarian law. the embargo should be in place until the end of hostilities and the resumption of negotiations.
in writing. ‒ this resolution, like the european union's 'human rights' ideology in international relations, is full of good sentiments, but has no idea of the background to the yemeni affair. it does not address the real issues that are shaking the conflict, and it evokes the implications of many harmful actors in the region (islamist terrorist groups). it does not mention the decisive role of saudi arabia and its allies in this conflict and takes a timid stance towards these actors, who are implicitly supported by eu member states. i therefore voted against this text.
in writing. ‒ i abstained on the resolution on the humanitarian situation in yemen. i am of course opposed to any acts which are contrary to fundamental rights and international law, and which are proven by neutral and independent actors. the situation in yemen is indeed unsustainable for a majority of civilians and a swift solution involving a political and democratic resolution for yemen must be found so that civilians, humanitarians and journalists no longer suffer the effects of this war. however, this resolution, by unilaterally and unbalancedly blaming the actors involved in the conflict, was unfortunately not in the direction of a solution to the crisis based on dialogue between all these actors. this resolution was adopted.
in writing. ‒ the humanitarian situation in yemen has become particularly dire since the intervention of a coalition of regional states against the houthi rebels. the conflict has left more than 6,000 dead, more than 30,000 wounded and 80 per cent of the yemeni population in need of humanitarian aid, according to the un. it is important that the european union and its parliament be the voice of respect for international law and fundamental rights. however, the aim of this resolution was more to punish and blame certain actors in this crisis than to really pacify the situation. i therefore abstained on this resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the resolution on the humanitarian situation in yemen. it is a text full of good sentiments, but it has no idea of the background of the yemeni case. i would like to denounce the postponement of the vote on this resolution, due to a mission of the foreign affairs committee of this parliament to saudi arabia which was to take place after the vote on this resolution at the first part-session in february. there is no point in voting resolutions if we do not even have the courage to defend them in front of the governments concerned.
in writing. ‒ the saudi coalition's intervention in yemen has resulted in more than 6,000 deaths, half of them civilians. this humanitarian crisis now affects 80 percent of the population. an expert report to the un security council indicates that the belligerents deliberately target civilian populations and infrastructure, in violation of international humanitarian law. the resolution therefore calls for a humanitarian truce and for investigations into allegations of violations of international law by saudi arabia and its allies. the socialists and democrats, through an amendment, wanted to go further by calling for the introduction of a european embargo on arms sales to saudi arabia. such a decision would be in line with the 2008 eu common position on arms exports, which requires member states, when exporting arms, to take into account the country of destination's compliance with international humanitarian law. i therefore vote in favour of this resolution because it sends a strong message to the belligerents.
in writing. ‒ the situation in yemen has worsened since the houthis took over the capital sanaa. at least 5,979 people have been killed since the conflict began and according to the humanitarian needs overview 2016 (hno) released in november 2015, 21.2 million people, or 82% of yemen's population, are in need of humanitarian assistance. the resolution condemns the 'saudi-led military intervention in yemen' and also condemns the eu member states for continuing to sell them arms, arguing that they are 'used to commit serious violations of international humanitarian law and to undermine regional peace, security and stability'. the resolution deplores the violations of the ceasefire and "stresses the need to coordinate humanitarian action under the auspices of the united nations". i am voting for this resolution which clearly denounces the actions of saudi arabia and is in line with the un.

on behalf of the enf group. mr president, the liberalisation of port services is an old european sea serpent. although the european commission has already suffered two failures in the early 2000s, it is back in charge: never two without three. the commission's proposal is unacceptable. on the one hand, it is trying to standardize the major european ports, which have different organizations, thus preventing member states and port managers from framing these services in the light of experience. on the other hand, under the pretext of competitiveness and with a view to attracting more investment, it emphasizes the need to liberalize certain services. this would have the harmful effect of preventing states from requiring certain services to be carried out under the national flag for security reasons. it is not possible to replace qualified seamen, pilots or tugboat operators with underqualified, underpaid people working on a ship flying a flag of convenience. the amendments by the committee on transport are positive, but in the end this regulation will be an empty shell. so why continue to harmonize and privatize at all costs? do we want our ports, which are strategic elements of our economy, to be bought up by foreign investors, as was the case recently with piraeus, which was taken over by the chinese group cosco? for these reasons we shall vote against the commission's proposal and against the european parliament's proposal.
commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this is the third time that the european commission has tried to impose the liberalisation of port services in europe. the name of the organization has been changed to 'port services organisation', but we are not to be fooled, this is again a matter of competing services such as loading, towing and steering in a whole range of ports, even though many of them are very different from each other. what works in rotterdam, hamburg or antwerp, which alone account for 20% of the transport of goods in europe, does not necessarily work in a port like le havre. unfortunately, your impact study does not take into account the specific features of the ports. what is worse, it imposes a uniform vision in disregard of reality, in disregard of people's experience, in disregard of environmental requirements, in disregard of social requirements. our objective should be to protect the coastlines and port safety on the one hand, but also to protect the workers on the other. all of this is now in jeopardy because of your project. the main demand of european ports is not liberalisation. what they are asking for is a clarification of european rules, for example on state aid. the commission has for years refused to publish specific guidelines on state aid to ports. even if some derogations from liberalisation were obtained in the negotiations, this text does not present enough safeguards, real progress, to be able to be supported. in these circumstances, we can only vote against this proposal.

in writing. ‒ the european parliament has adopted new rules to better prevent and stop outbreaks of serious animal diseases such as avian influenza and african swine fever. the adoption of this new legislation simplifies a regulation that is more than 50 years old, and i welcome this, as it is an important victory that strengthens citizen democracy by putting the main actors back at the heart of the system in the development of emergency plans. the increase in trade, climate change and the mutation of infectious agents are now increasing the risk of the emergence of previously unknown diseases such as avian influenza, which is now affecting the entire palm tree sector very severely. as such, i can only welcome the strengthening of prevention and biosecurity to protect not only animal health but also human health and the environment. however, the available budget for financing health measures in case of crisis remains largely insufficient. it is essential that the european commission implement a compensation mechanism that allows for a swift response to the violence of these crises and their health, economic and human impact. unfortunately, prevention is not the answer.

in writing. ‒ the aim of this report is to establish a single framework for the prevention and control of animal diseases transmissible to animals and humans and to establish a harmonised animal health strategy. while the community acquis currently consists of 50 basic directives and regulations, as well as some 400 secondary legislation, this text is therefore of crucial importance in terms of simplification but also in a difficult health context in france (blue-blooded sheep fever and avian influenza) and in europe (swine fever). the report, in addition to establishing a single framework of provisions, emphasises the responsibility of actors and basic knowledge of health risks, the notification and monitoring of health risks to control diseases, the obligation for member states to develop response plans to deal with certain and to carry out simulation exercises, the registration, approval, traceability and movements of terrestrial, aquatic or other types of animals and the standards and requirements applicable to exports and third countries dispatching animals and products of animal origin in order to prevent the introduction of animal diseases into the union. i voted in favour of this text.

in writing. ‒ harmonised indices of consumer prices (hicps) are a measure of inflation providing valuable information on the deflation of economic values such as wages, rents and interest rates. they therefore form the basis for decisions on economic and monetary policy. i voted in favour of this resolution because it makes it possible to establish harmonised, and therefore comparable, statistics between the member states and thus to better coordinate economic and monetary measures within the union.
in writing. ‒ the harmonised index of consumer prices (hicp) is an index of consumer prices (cpi) calculated for each of the countries of the european union and a few other european countries. it is used by the ecb as an indicator of price stability and as a means of checking compliance with the inflation convergence criterion. the amendments introduced would establish a common framework for the development, production and dissemination of the harmonised index of consumer prices, the harmonised index of consumer prices at constant tax rate (hicp-tc), the owner-occupied housing price index (lop) and the property price index (hipi) at union, national and sub-national level. it is a mainly technical amendment to the regulation to take better account of price variations across member states. however, these indices can be used as policy tools to better control member states by imposing targets on them... or to regain imaginary growth by changing the calculation formulas. that's why i abstained.

in writing. ‒ this report is a proposal to amend the regulation on consumer price indices. this price index allows the level of inflation to be calculated in the most comparable way for all countries and is used by the european central bank as an indicator of price stability and as a means of checking compliance with the inflation convergence criterion. the amendments introduced would establish a common framework for the development, production and dissemination of the harmonised index of consumer prices (hicp), the harmonised index of consumer prices at constant tax rate (hicp-tc), the owner-occupied housing price index (lop), and the property price index (hipi) at union, national and sub-national level. however, caution is needed as these indices can be used as policy tools to better control member states by imposing targets, or to regain imaginary growth by changing the calculation formulas. one of the two proposed packages of amendments was adopted, giving far too much power to the european commission. i therefore voted against.

in writing. the commission is today presenting its proposal for a targeted revision of the 'posting' directive. the principle would be that a posted worker would receive the same pay as a local worker, including bonuses and other benefits. it is undoubtedly favourable to the posted worker, if not to the unemployed national, but frankly i do not see how it solves the problem of social dumping and unfair competition. because this competition also lies in a difference in cost. in france, even if their wages are the same, a romanian or polish posted worker will still cost less than a french or immigrant worker. and this will always give foreign companies a competitive advantage over their french competitors in order to win markets, such as the organisation of the ps summer universities or cop21, for example. it would also be a question of limiting the duration of the secondment to two years, which is already a huge amount, with the automatic transformation of the posted worker into an immigrant worker after this period. and frankly, the consequences are staggering. i am waiting to see the exact wording of your proposals. you yourself have said, commissioner, that you want more posted workers, more crossborder service provision. that 's the problem !
in writing. the european commission has today presented its proposal for a revision of the rules governing the posting of workers within the union. it was time, when we know that the current directive has reached the canonical age of 20 years. while the 1996 directive was designed to protect employees, it has been largely diverted from its objective, opening the way to widespread social and fiscal competition between workers, enterprises and social protection systems. at first sight, several of the proposals in this project are interesting: posted workers should enjoy the same pay conditions as their colleagues working for the same company under a contract from the host country. they should also be entitled to the thirteenth month, christmas or seniority bonuses if they exist in the sector in which they are employed. however, these proposals do not eliminate all forms of abuse. this is particularly the case with social security contributions and the portability of rights acquired by the employee in the host country. this review, which has now been initiated, is giving new impetus to the debate on the fight against social dumping. social europe is the sine qua non for the future of the european project.

in writing. ‒ this directive clearly falls within the competence of the member states. everything is being done to complicate the procedures for minors. i therefore voted against this text.
in writing. ‒ in the european union, an estimated one million children are subject to criminal proceedings. however, there are considerable and worrying differences between member states in the treatment of children involved in these procedures. the rights of the child are not sufficiently guaranteed within the union and have been the subject of numerous judgments by the european court of human rights. for all these reasons, and in order to improve the treatment of children in court, i voted in favour of this legislative resolution.
in writing. ‒ the european commission estimates that one million children are subject to criminal proceedings in the european union, representing 12% of all those subject to criminal proceedings. the report does not mention that a large proportion of juvenile crime is linked to immigration. this directive will make procedures more cumbersome and complicated, and procedural errors more likely. the european union is also working on a common criminal law, although this is a matter for the member states. so i was logically opposed to this new attack on the sovereignty of france... and the other member states.
in writing. ‒ this text gives us an opportunity to welcome europe's intervention. this proposal for a directive is very positive in many respects. the desire to ensure, through common minimum standards, effective and sufficiently uniform access for minors to the right to a fair trial at all stages of the proceedings must be a fundamental right beyond doubt. unfortunately, it is clear that the rights of the child in the various stages of criminal proceedings are not sufficiently guaranteed within the union at present. they have even led to numerous convictions of member states by the european court of human rights. for example, in some countries children do not have the fundamental right to be assisted by a lawyer. this should be a child's inalienable right. i therefore support the general approach of this report and many of its proposals and i voted in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ i opposed this report, which is merely an attempt to create a european criminal law by proposing the introduction of procedural safeguards for children, which already exist in every state that respects the law. while everyone can understand the need for a right to information or the compulsory assistance of a lawyer for minors who are being prosecuted, this directive will only make the procedures more burdensome and complicated, even though such rights are already in force in france. moreover, while the european commission estimates that one million children are subject to criminal proceedings in the eu - 12% of those subject to such proceedings - it fails to note the statistical links between juvenile delinquency and immigration. in view of the commission's attempt to violate one of the three fundamental pillars of our political system, and the naivety of the drafters of this text, i could only vote against it.
in writing. ‒ with this directive, the european union is developing criminal law, an area which falls within the exclusive competence of the member states. the text will also make procedures more cumbersome and complicated and make procedural errors more likely. i therefore voted against.
in writing. ‒ the purpose of this proposal for a directive is to provide safeguards for individuals aged between 18 and 21 years who are prosecuted in criminal proceedings where the alleged offence was committed before the age of 18. the text provides for a number of rights for suspects, such as the right to information, the right to mandatory assistance by a lawyer at every stage of the proceedings and the right to be the subject of a personalised assessment to take better account of the social environment in which the suspect has evolved. through this directive, the european union is beginning to develop a common criminal law, thus violating the principle of subsidiarity in so far as this is a matter for the member states. that is why i voted against this text.

in writing. ‒ since 2004, the member states and the commission have had a cooperation agreement with philip morris to combat illicit trade in tobacco products. they get $1.25 billion over 12 years and in return, they drop all lawsuits against philip morris. the socialist and democratic group firmly opposed the renewal of this cooperation agreement, which was coming to an end, and obtained a decision from parliament to that effect. it was in contravention of article 5.3 of the who framework convention on tobacco control, which calls for limiting interactions with tobacco companies. moreover, this agreement was far removed from the realities of the market which is beyond its reach. other tools exist to combat illicit tobacco trade and are provided for in the 2014 directive and the who protocol against illicit tobacco trade: traceability, production of quantities absorbable by the legal market. i therefore voted in favour of this resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution which opposes the renewal of an agreement concluded in 2004 between the european commission and philip morris, the world's leading cigarette manufacturer, to combat smuggling and counterfeiting. this agreement established a conflict of interest relationship: philip morris provided financial resources to the european union anti-fraud office, and in return, fought against the smuggling and counterfeiting of tobacco products. apart from ethical issues, the effectiveness of such agreements is questionable in view of the increase in the trade in cheap white cigarettes. the non-extension of this agreement is in line with the principles of the tobacco directive adopted in 2014 and avoids any conflict of interest situation. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the 2014 tobacco products directive, which provides for a number of instruments to combat smuggling. it is also crucial that member states ratify the protocol to the who framework convention on tobacco control which obliges parties to protect their public health policies from the commercial interests of the tobacco industry.
in writing. ‒ the european socialists are determined to fight the tobacco lobby. in 2004, the commission and the member states concluded a 'cooperation' agreement with philip morris international, which had committed to pay €1.2 billion over 12 years to compensate for the damage caused by the illicit tobacco trade in europe. the agreement expires in july and the european parliament has voted to not renew it. the tobacco industry's funding of public institutions is an anomaly which we had to correct, since it contravenes the framework convention of the world health organization. moreover, this agreement no longer corresponds to illegal tobacco practices, since we are seeing an increase in the production of 'cheap whites', that is to say unsealed cigarettes produced outside the european union. while philip morris has used all its lobbying power to fight the 2014 tobacco directive, and the company is not backing down from any obstacles to its transposition, we refuse to renew this agreement. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the problem of tobacco use.
in writing. ‒ this resolution deals with the regulation of the tobacco trade. smuggling in this area is estimated to cost member states up to €10 billion in unpaid taxes, often to fund criminal activities. several cooperation agreements now require the tobacco industry to set up product controls and monitoring and to limit sales according to demand. these agreements also contain provisions which are now incompatible with european legislation on the presentation and sale of cigarette packets. one of the agreements expires in july 2016. while this agreement may have been useful at the time it was concluded in 2004, the significant changes that have occurred in the regulatory framework no longer justify its renewal. the elements relating to illicit trade in tobacco will in any case be covered by the tobacco products directive and the protocol to the who framework convention on tobacco control. i voted against the renewal of such an agreement, which could be derogated from, and for the report.

i'm the reporter. madam president, i hope my colleagues have had time to get into the chamber, because i would like to begin by thanking very warmly my fictitious colleagues and the teams of commissioner andriukaitis who have worked with me on this dossier. with over 1 000 amendments and almost 150 articles, it was a titanic task, which we accomplished as a team, in a spirit of cooperation and compromise which i very much appreciated. this was necessary in view of the important issues involved in this legislative revision. with the world health organization warning that the world may be heading for a post-antibiotic era, where antibiotic resistance kills more people each year than cancer, it was time to take decisive action and get to the root of the problem. the fight against antibiotic resistance must indeed start on the farm. the report calls for a ban on the purely preventive use of antibiotics, for restricting mass treatment to very specific cases, for a ban on the veterinary use of antibiotics critical for human medicine and for an end to the online sale of antibiotics, vaccines and psychotropic products. with these measures, we hope to reduce the amount of antibiotics that end up on consumers' plates. however, we must not reduce the therapeutic arsenal of veterinarians. they are responsible professionals, who we must trust. they are best placed to choose the most appropriate treatment for the circumstances. this regulation is designed to facilitate their work and not to over-regulate a profession which has already demonstrated its commitment to high ethical rigor. it should also be stressed that there is a real problem of availability of medicines on the veterinary market. to protect animal health, the quality of treatment must be improved and the use of medicinal products not authorised for placing on the market reduced. to do this, it is absolutely necessary to encourage research and innovation in this sector. our report is therefore very ambitious in this respect. it proposes extending certain periods of commercial exclusivity, in particular for medicines intended for minor species, in order to create strong incentives for research. the burden of administrative procedures, particularly in terms of pharmacovigilance, is another obstacle to the marketing of innovative products. on the basis of the commission's proposals, we have therefore revised certain provisions in order to create a new pharmacovigilance system which is more flexible, more efficient and less bureaucratic. accelerated procedures must also allow laboratories to react quickly to, for example, animal disease without compromising our quality and safety standards, which are among the highest in the world. finally, this new regulation must first and foremost serve the interests of farmers and herders, whose present difficulties we are aware of and who will be the first to be affected by this text. the rules in this legislation are not intended to stigmatize them, but to help them and to take better care of their herds. i wanted in particular to ensure, with our colleagues in the committee on agriculture and the farmers' unions, that these new rules are applicable on the ground and do not add to the administrative burden they are already suffering from. in conclusion, the main challenge was threefold: protection of animal health and therefore of human health, the fight against antibiotic resistance and the competitiveness of our farms and our veterinary medicines industry, objectives which may seem contradictory, but which we have managed to perfectly reconcile in this legislative report. i now wish we were wasting no more time. parliament is ready. the council is in the ballpark and i would be delighted to hear from my colleagues.

member of the commission.– mr president, i would like to thank roberto gualtieri very much for this report on the banking union. i think he gave us an excellent reminder of how much has been achieved as we have worked to overhaul europe’s regulatory and supervisory framework in recent years. the banking union is absolutely central to this new architecture. the single supervisor and the single resolution authority already feel very well established, and it is easy to forget now that the transition of supervisory tasks from national authorities to the ssm only took place one year ago, or that the single resolution board only became fully operational in january this year. so we have taken big steps forward, delivered in record time. we have helped make europe’s banks stronger and better capitalised, and europe’s taxpayers better protected. i would like to thank members of this committee, and also my predecessor, for the part that they have all played in this. the report covers a lot of ground, so i will just highlight some of the main points raised by mr gualtieri. we agree on the need, both at eu level and of course within member states, to tackle the non-performing loans that continue to weigh negatively on parts of the banking sector. i very much agree that we must check that our legislation is proportionate, that it is sensitive to different business models, and that it avoids unnecessary compliance requirements, particularly for the smaller banks. that is what we will look at in our review of the crr. i also agree that we need to do everything we can to support lending to smes and long-term investment in infrastructure projects. so far as strengthening the banking union is concerned, here the main focus is on our proposal to create a european deposit insurance scheme (edis) by 2024, and that is a key part of the broader plan to deepen economic and monetary union. it will give the banking union the third leg that was always intended. we have sought to come up with a balanced approach, an approach that seeks to reduce risk as well as to mutualise it. it is vital that we pursue both sides of this equation in parallel. we need to keep up the pressure to ensure that the bank recovery and resolution directive and the deposit guarantee scheme directive are fully transposed into national legislation. we are nearly there on that. we will soon consult on the key differences in insolvency and early restructuring regimes across the eu and we will come forward before the end of the year with a proposal to apply the total loss-absorbing capacity (tlac) standard in a way that works for europe. mr gualtieri highlighted a moment ago in his remarks his concerns about the pillar 2 capital requirements for banks and their relationship with the capital buffers. we know that there are differences in how these rules are applied by supervisors and that is why we have now started the process of reflecting on this with member states and here in the parliament and with others, so that the legislation can work as it was originally intended. there needs to be a clearer difference between the goals of pillar 1 requirements that apply to all banks and pillar 2 requirements that are institution-specific and depend on the level of additional risk that banks bear. i am very grateful for what mr gualtieri said and i look forward to continuing the discussion on this very important issue. so these were just some of the areas that struck me in the report. i share the view that we have got strong foundations on which to build and, overall, i am optimistic about the opportunity we have to refine our legislation so that we can continue to meet our prudential objectives while also supporting growth and investment in europe.

in writing. ‒ i took a position against this text on emergency trade measures for tunisia. while i believe that tunisia should be a strategic partner, particularly for france, because of the historical ties between our two countries, and i am aware of the destabilisation of the tunisian economy by terrorist attacks, i do not believe that putting our european olive growers in competition with the tunisian olive oil industry is the solution to tunisia's economic problems. of course, we must help tunisia to stabilize, in particular to avoid the risk of political and social upheavals which would also have a serious impact on the europeans, but the proposed aid would remove customs duties on an additional 35 000 tonnes of olive oil, even though our agricultural sector is experiencing one of the most serious crises in its history and the price of olive oil has been falling substantially for the last ten years. it would have been necessary to provide tunisia with strategic support, in particular to revitalise the tourist sector, but this solution will have, at best, only short-term beneficial effects for the tunisians and most certainly catastrophic effects for european olive growers, especially italian, spanish, but also french.
in writing. ‒ following the terrorist attacks in sousse, tunisia in september 2015, the tunisian economy, which is heavily dependent on tourism, was significantly impacted. with this in mind, the commission has proposed the unilateral and temporary establishment of a tariff quota of 35 000 tonnes per year for olive oil exports from tunisia to the european union for a period of two years. at the february plenary session in brussels, the european parliament called for additional measures to guarantee protection for european olive oil producers. the latter are mainly located in the southern regions of the union which are experiencing significant economic difficulties. it was therefore necessary to implement a measure which would be both beneficial for tunisia and not endanger european olive oil producers. i voted in favour of this text, which is a perfectly acceptable compromise.
in writing. ‒ i opposed this exemption from customs duties for the export of tens of thousands of tonnes of tunisian oil, voting against this text. our duty as parliamentarians is to protect our olive growers first. the latter are particularly affected by the xylella bacteria, particularly in corsica, italy being even more severely affected. not to mention spain, whose production has been weakened by drought since 2013. the exemption of tunisia is a bonus when we know that it is already benefiting greatly from the recent increase in oil prices, which is precisely the result of this context.
in writing. ‒ i voted against: the european union could have helped tunisia in other ways without putting european olive growers in difficulty.
in writing. ‒ tunisia, which has been hit by terrorist attacks since 2015, has experienced a significant decline in the number of visitors to its tourist sites, which are particularly important for its economy. the union is responding with this resolution to its promise made last year to explore the possibility of taking exceptional and temporary measures vis-à-vis tunisia. that is why it seems to me a sensible move to allow the import of 70 000 tonnes of olive oil duty free into the union. these trade measures are a good way for the union to support the tunisian economy, especially since they are subject to compliance with control rules. finally, these measures are limited in time and resources are left to the commission in the event of an imbalance on the european olive oil market. this well thought-out resolution will make it possible to implement an excellent aid measure for tunisia without risking damage to the union, and that is why i voted for it without hesitation.
in writing. to help tunisia, whose economy is severely affected by the terrorist attacks, the commission proposes an additional tariff-free quota of 35 000 tonnes of olive oil exports from tunisia to the union. the current quota is 56 700 tonnes. the measure will be implemented from 1 january 2016 to 31 december 2017. tunisia is experiencing serious difficulties following the numerous attacks that have shaken its tourism sector. we need help to prevent the regime from being toppled and this country, so close to us, from being destabilised. the aid proposed is to put an additional 35 000 tonnes of olive oil at zero customs duty. the european union could have helped tunisia in other ways without putting european olive growers in difficulty. the price of olive oil has been falling for the last 10 years, affecting european producers, without the commission being concerned. i therefore voted against this text.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report by my colleague, mrs marielle de sarnez, on the introduction of emergency autonomous trade measures for tunisia. the aim is to exempt from customs duties a quota of exports of tunisian olive oil. these measures are temporary and exceptional and an impact analysis on european producers will be carried out mid-term. olive oil is one of the only sources of agricultural exports from tunisia to the european union, whose sector supports more than a million people. it is important to support tunisia and thus its democratic process which, while being one of the most advanced in the region, is threatened by significant security challenges, making it essential to support the stability of the tunisian economy. i welcome the fact that this text was adopted by a large majority.
in writing. to help the tunisian economy, the commission proposed to grant us 35,000 tonnes of import quotas without customs duties for tunisian olive oil for the years 2016 and 2017. these quotas have, however, been strongly criticised by farmers in the south of the european union. they have just suffered a drop in production due to a bacterial attack on olive trees, and they are worried about seeing tunisian olive oil take the market share they have lost. since these doubts have not received clear answers from the commission and since the amendments i tabled calling for safeguard measures for producers have not been adopted, i decided to abstain, since i also did not want to block a measure which could help the tunisian economy. i would point out, however, that there are many other ways of helping the tunisian economy, starting with the revision of its debt or the conditions we attach to our financial aid, rather than taking measures which threaten european producers and set them against tunisian ones.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the introduction of emergency trade measures for tunisia. the country, which has been the victim of terrorism, has seen its tourism industry decline. at the same time, the olive oil sector is important for tunisia, olive oil being its main agricultural export product. the granting of a unilateral tariff quota of 35 000 tonnes free of customs duties for exports of olive oil from tunisia is therefore a way for europe to show its support for the country, and this on a temporary basis (2 years). above all, no disturbance of the european olive oil market is to be expected, particularly in france where tunisian olive oil does not compete with french oils, which are protected by geographical indications. trade can be a weapon, but it can also be a shield.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the legislative resolution which closes the first reading and allows the autonomous emergency trade measures for tunisia to enter into force very soon, given that an agreement with the council has been reached. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the conclusion of the agreement on the free movement of goods between the european community and tunisia. this measure will provide support to tunisia to help revive its economy, which has been severely destabilised by the terrorist attacks. the agreement reached with the council endorses the parliament's position, which stresses the importance of ensuring that there is no abuse or circumvention of this additional quota and that it benefits all tunisian producers, including small producers. it also sets up a mid-term review of the effects of this regulation in order to be able to take corrective measures to restore the situation on the european market should it be destabilised. i welcome the adoption of this agreement, which demonstrates the union's support for tunisia in pursuing its democratic transition.

in writing. ‒ the report aims to temporarily increase the quotas for importing tunisian olive oil into the european union. tunisia's economy is in tatters after the tourism slump that followed the attacks. this quota is a drop in the bucket (35 000 tonnes per year) compared to european production (more than 1 million tonnes), but it is a breath of fresh air for the tunisian economy. the new quotas are also very time-bound (maximum 2 years) and are accompanied by a mid-term evaluation (with an update if their consequences prove harmful) and a 'monitoring clause' (the obligation to ensure that all olive oil is produced entirely in the country and transported directly from tunisia). these measures are therefore not likely to destabilise the european market and will not solve the problems of farmers in southern europe (italy and spain) related to olive tree diseases and the practices of the european agri-food industry. they are vital to help tunisia's successful democratic transition. i voted yes.

in writing. ‒ the objective of this report is to simplify the legislation on veterinary medicinal products by merging the directive establishing a community code relating to veterinary medicinal products with the regulation establishing community procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human and veterinary use. the new text will make it possible to combat the misuse of antibiotics in livestock farming. the sale and prescription of antibiotics for veterinary use will be greatly reduced and more controlled. legislation is needed to deal with the new phenomenon of antibiotic resistance. the amount of antibiotics we consume through our diet causes a certain addiction that makes these antibiotics less effective at treating us when we're sick. i voted for this text, which is the european parliament's position in negotiations with the member states.
in writing. ‒ the aim of this legislative report is to revise the 2004 legislation on veterinary medicines. the text covers the authorisation, production, sale, distribution and use of veterinary medicinal products during their life cycle. it aims in particular to improve access to medical products for professionals and to encourage innovation. the harmonization of veterinary prescription conditions and mutual recognition between member states will create a level playing field between countries and a minimum level of health security. the text also provides for the facilitation of the circulation of veterinary medicinal products throughout the union, while reducing the use of antibiotics in livestock farming. considering that this report facilitates the safe access of veterinary medicines via online purchase for farmers and their prescription by veterinarians, i voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ in the context of the revision of the veterinary medicines regulation, it is planned to centralize authorisations as much as possible with a single european agency. the report therefore amends the commission proposal on the separation of the veterinary and human activities of the european medicines agency. some of the rapporteur's proposals are in the right direction, including stricter monitoring by parliament, but the objective remains the same: to centralize as much as possible and to remove power and expertise from the member states by transferring competences. i therefore voted against.
in writing. ‒ this report sets out parliament's position on the european commission's new draft regulation on veterinary medicines, which aims to introduce administrative simplifications. parliament called for the fight against the growing resistance of bacteria to current antibiotics and for the prohibition of collective and preventive antibiotic treatment of animals, as well as for better differentiation between the veterinary and human medicines markets, in particular by the establishment of a list of critically important antibiotics for human use. this report could have gone further, however. our group tabled amendments to reduce the time taken by patent monopolies and to make generic medicines more easily available at lower prices, but they were rejected. we have advocated and obtained strong environmental and animal protection as criteria on impact assessment and the ban on online sales for antibiotics, vaccines and psychotropic products. it should be noted that member states are free to go further if they wish. i voted in favour of this report and i was surprised to find that the national front had rejected the administrative simplifications which it proposed.

in writing. ‒ this annual report on the banking union by the econ committee focuses on the three pillars of the banking union: the single supervisory mechanism (ssm), the single resolution mechanism (srm), and deposit protection. the report also calls for the establishment of a european supervisory authority to monitor the implementation of the euro. on the mru, the report welcomes the establishment of national resolution authorities and stresses that the single resolution board (srb) should, as a matter of priority, define the resolution plans for systemically important institutions... left to the sole discretion of the ecb, etc. in short, another report of self-satisfaction that accompanies the permanent communication operation of the eurocrats. however, the reforms that have been put in place are far from what is needed to limit the power of the banks to cause harm. eight years after the crisis, the banking system has only grown, especially in the shadow banking sector.

in writing. ‒ the banking union is europe's response to the economic and financial crisis of 2008. the banking union is built on three pillars: the single supervisory mechanism, the single resolution mechanism and the european deposit guarantee scheme. the first two pillars have recently been put in place. they help to prevent potential crises by monitoring the behaviour of banks and to be prepared in the event of a proven crisis to ensure that the european economy is as little affected as possible. the final pillar has yet to be determined. this should provide additional insurance for savers. discussions on this third pillar of the banking union are currently under way in the european parliament. i voted in favour of this text, which is parliament's first report on the banking union.
in writing. ‒ this report presents the european parliament's position on the state of the banking union in its 2015 annual report. we call on the european commission and the supervisors to consider solutions to increase the lending capacity of the european union. the commission's proposal is to increase the union's own resources. the report also discusses the proposed deposit guarantee scheme, which aims to secure people's savings in banks. i voted in favour of the report, in support of these objectives.

in writing. ‒ i voted against: this is a communication operation, the reforms put in place are far from what is needed to limit the power of the banks to cause harm.
in writing. ‒ the 2008 crisis exposed what we had suspected: the irresponsibility of the financial sector, and even its potential to harm the real economy. i fear that despite some regulatory efforts, including at european level, this has not changed. you also took advantage of the situation, as usual, to give a little more power to the european level, with the banking union. the aim is to centralise the supervision of euro area credit institutions and decisions on their rescue in the event of default, breaking the link between sovereign states and national banks. and from now on, it's the bank's customers who will be called upon to bail them out. but you do not get to the heart of the matter: without the banking separation, which you reject, the banks will continue to speculate with depositors' money; you don't seriously tackle shadow banking, which banks use to circumvent your prudential rules; the ecb keeps pumping more liquidity into the markets, but it's not benefiting the real economy. as long as you put yourself at the service of finance rather than forcing finance to be at the service of the economy, nothing will move forward.
in writing. this report therefore gives an overview of the progress made in banking union and the remaining weaknesses. it should also be noted that, eight years after the crisis, the banking system has only grown, especially in the shadow banking sector. although the ssm has improved supervision of banks and capital requirements have been increased, banks still pose a huge threat to the global economy. in addition, no details were provided on the resolution of systemic banks. beyond a balance sheet of eur 30 billion, resolution is the responsibility of the ecb and not the mru. the work done by the european institutions in the framework of the banking union is a communication operation designed to make it appear that the european union is taking the bull by the horns. the reforms that have been put in place are far from what is needed to limit the power of the banks to cause harm. the first of these measures should be to separate retail and investment activities in order to protect deposits, which is categorically rejected by the european union. i therefore voted against this text.

on behalf of the enf group. mr president, the yellow card procedure is the main weapon used by national parliaments to force the commission in brussels to respect the principle of subsidiarity. it obliges the commission to reconsider a legislative proposal when it has been the subject of reasoned opinions, i.e. objections from one third of the national parliaments of the member states. the report notes that this yellow card has only once succeeded in persuading the commission to abandon a proposal. it was in 2012, about the scandalous monti ii proposal, which called into question the right to strike. it is a very meagre balance sheet because the commission has been arrogantly rejecting the other yellow cards for the rest of the time. subsidiarity is therefore a decoy. the commission does not respect it and violates it, either directly or indirectly, by means of delegated acts, that is to say, by means of decree-laws, which it uses massively, as the report deplores. the report does have the merit of denouncing this situation, but it is disappointing in that it merely calls on the commission to engage in a dialogue with national parliaments and to improve its impact studies. he proposed the creation of a green card, which would allow national parliaments to make suggestions to the commission, but this would only revive the old regime placards which the commanders presented to the king's pleasure. it is a much more radical and democratic solution that should be put in place. it would be to create a genuine red card procedure which would allow each member state to oppose a commission legislative proposal if it considers that proposal to be prejudicial to its vital interest. this red card would be a veto right which would allow each state to enforce its sovereignty. it would thus be a first step towards replacing the european union with the europe of nations, which i wish to see.

mr president, commissioner, i have the impression that we are being unreasonable. it is almost a year since we in this house have been talking about the crisis, it is more than a year since farmers have been reporting on the situation, it is more than a year since all the economic players in the sectors have been warning us and, despite all this, despite all the measures that have been taken, nothing has changed on the farms. the european parliament voted over 70% in favour of a mechanism to limit production in times of crisis. this kind of mechanism can only succeed if it applies to all european countries. it is not agricultural policy to leave a choice to the card in times of crisis, because crises are general; it is not agricultural policy to shift the burden of financing accompanying measures onto the member states, especially since the de minimis ceiling will not be raised for a very long time. the commission as a whole - and not just you, who have become aware of the problems - must wake up, commissioner, or agriculture will have disappeared from a number of our territories before the end of this parliamentary term.
mr president, commissioner, i still think that you and the commission have not grasped the scale of the crisis. the answers you give are far from the realities that occupy us every day. it is not by using article 222 in a partial way, as you put it, that we will respond to the intensity and difficulty of the economic situation. as has just been said, article 222 had to be applied in its entirety and these regulatory measures applied to all farmers in all the member states of the union. this required additional resources. that is my view at the time of our discussions. i would also like to draw your attention, commissioner, to the negotiations currently taking place between the european union and mercosur. you must categorically refuse any offer including sensitive products and, in particular, beef. it is not possible to consider livestock farming, which is experiencing an unprecedented structural economic crisis, as a variable for adjustment to the commission's trade agreements. this is the case for our model of society and the european project itself.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, your committee on agriculture wanted to start the trilogue negotiations after the vote on this text. this is the first time that the report has been discussed in plenary. i would like to thank the negotiating team and our partners in the other institutions. the list of votes proposed is therefore the result of the negotiation. if one of the amendments tabled by a political group in plenary were adopted, the political agreement would fall. i therefore ask you to reject the amendments proposed by one political group.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the walesa report on the arrangements applicable to products originating in certain african, caribbean and pacific (acp) states covered by economic partnership agreements (recast). rewording is a technique which aims to codify in a single legal act legislative provisions which have been amended several times, in order to facilitate access to and reading of them, while making substantive changes to the text. in order to recognise the substantive changes introduced in the text, these are highlighted in grey in the commission proposal. article 104 of parliament's rules of procedure explains the procedure for the recasting: the text concerned is referred to the committee responsible for the subject-matter and to the committee on legal affairs. the legal services of the three institutions (european parliament, council and commission) meet and examine the drafting proposals.

in writing. - i voted against this bill. european vat systems are supposed to be subject to european harmonisation. pending a directive to this effect, a provisional scheme has been introduced: it sets a minimum standard rate of 15% applicable to all member states for the period 2011-2015. the commission proposes to extend this transitional regime until 2017. at the same time, its proposals on european vat are expected to be published in the course of 2016. we are opposed to any harmonisation of taxation at european union level. taxation is a prerogative of sovereign states, and the setting of rates depends on factors specific to each of them.
in writing. ‒ the minimum vat rates are justified by the fact that vat is still levied in several cases on the principle of origin rather than on the principle of destination (in particular crossborder short distance purchases and sales). therefore, the application of a minimum rate in all member states, as is currently the case, makes it possible to prevent any tax dumping and is a useful guarantee for the proper functioning of the internal market. in addition, all member states now apply a standard rate of more than 15%; the extension of the 15% threshold therefore also provides a margin of manoeuvre for member states to carry out vat reforms, for example to reduce the standard rate by broadening the vat base and limiting the use of reduced rates. in these circumstances, and pending a major communication from the european commission on vat due in 2016, it is indeed prudent to extend the standard minimum vat rate of 15% and to maintain the current provisions for a period of three years (until 31 december 2018). i voted in favour of this necessary adjustment.
in writing. ‒ article 113 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union provides that the council is to adopt provisions on the harmonisation of legislation on turnover taxes, in so far as such harmonisation is necessary to ensure the establishment and functioning of the internal market and to avoid distortions of competition. the report proposes to maintain the common minimum standard vat rate in the union at 15% until 2018. in fact, since 1993 the normal vat rate has not been lower than 15%. however, the most unjust tax is the value-added tax (vat), which is paid by everyone, regardless of income. an ambitious tax policy should tackle this tax, which will be impossible in this context. in a time of widespread tax evasion, there is much better to do. i vote against it.

in writing. ‒ while the principle of subsidiarity, enshrined in article 5 of the treaty on european union, is fundamental to decision-making within the union in that it aims to determine the most relevant level of intervention in areas of shared competence, as is the principle of proportionality which derives from it, this report does nothing to ensure that it is more faithfully respected. while denouncing the commission's rejection of the yellow card procedures whereby national parliaments invite the commission to reconsider a legislative proposal when it has been the subject of 'reasoned opinions' protests by one third of the national parliaments of the member states , it merely calls on the commission to engage in a dialogue with the national parliaments, and rejects the introduction of a veto, a red card which would actually enshrine the principle of subsidiarity. i have opposed this report because it refuses to take the necessary steps to enforce a fundamental principle, a blatant failure of eurocratic fraud.
in writing. ‒ i voted without hesitation in favour of my british colleague's report. it is time someone reminded our assembly of the importance of the principle of subsidiarity in the legislative work of our institutions. this is an important point which we tend to forget, or even deny, because subsidiarity is one of the last weapons left to european nations when their interests do not correspond to the dictates which the commission wants to impose on them. and subsidiarity - have we forgotten? - is enshrined in the maastricht treaty, adopted more than 25 years ago. it was even with the principle of subsidiarity that the then recalcitrant citizens of my country were convinced to vote in favour of maastricht in the referendum organised by françois mitterrand. the socialists have now tried, in a subtle way, to change the substance of the report to remove the principle of subsidiarity. europe will only survive if the institutions understand that subsidiarity must remain the foundation on which legislation can be built that benefits all europeans without harming the interests of the member states.

in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report deals with the annual reports on subsidiarity and proportionality. it sets out the state of play of the procedures and mechanisms for monitoring the subsidiarity and proportionality of national parliaments. the rapporteur stresses the importance of political dialogue between the national and european institutions and the possibility for national parliaments to propose the adoption, amendment or rejection of certain legislative provisions. i have supported this report because i believe that cooperation between national and european institutions improves respect for the competences of the member states and promotes the effective implementation of standards.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report. the principles of proportionality and subsidiarity are fundamental principles of the european union. it is essential that these two principles be respected and that the institutions and national parliaments ensure this through careful scrutiny. in order to reduce the democratic deficit, it is crucial that in-depth subsidiarity impact assessments are carried out by the commission with a view to increasing the confidence of citizens and businesses.
in writing. ‒ in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, enshrined in article 5 teu, the european union can only intervene if it is able to act more effectively than the member states at national or local level. the report regrets the ineffectiveness of the yellow card procedure, which is the main tool used by national parliaments to force the commission in brussels to respect the principle of subsidiarity. it also deplored the massive use of 'delegated acts', i.e. commission decree-laws. unfortunately, the report merely calls on the commission to engage with national parliaments and improve its impact studies. i voted against the report because it is a frank statement but does not respect the sovereignty of the nations.
in writing. ‒ vote against: this red card would be a veto right which would allow each state to enforce its sovereignty.
in writing. ‒ the yellow card procedure is the main tool used by national parliaments to force the brussels commission to respect the principle of subsidiarity. it obliges the commission to reconsider a legislative proposal when it has been the subject of 'reasoned opinions', i.e. protests, by one third of the national parliaments of the member states. subsidiarity is therefore a decoy. the commission does not respect it and violates it either directly or indirectly by means of 'delegated acts', i.e. decree-laws, which it uses massively, as the report deplores. the report has the merit of denouncing this situation. but it is disappointing that it merely calls on the commission to engage in dialogue with national parliaments and to improve its impact studies. the commission's proposal is to be implemented by a new procedure, the 'red card' procedure, which would allow each member state to oppose a commission legislative proposal if it considers that it is contrary to its vital interests. i voted against this text.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the 2012 and 2013 annual reports on subsidiarity and proportionality proposed by my colleague sajjad karim. the report highlights the fact that extensive impact assessments that assess compliance with subsidiarity in a thorough manner are essential to improve citizens' confidence. i have endorsed this commission proposal which helps decision-makers to assess whether legislation is in line with eu principles and improves transparency on the outcome of negotiation periods. this resolution was adopted by a large majority, which i welcome.
in writing. ‒ this text dealt with two commission reports on the application of the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality in the european union, and in particular on the link with national parliaments and on the use of impact assessments in the legislative procedure at european level. the report suggests, in particular, that national parliaments should be better integrated into the legislative process. i voted in favour of this text because it is balanced.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the reports on subsidiarity and proportionality. the principle of subsidiarity is fundamental. the eu can only intervene if it is able to act more effectively than the member states. the yellow card procedure is the main tool used by national parliaments to force the commission to respect this principle. it obliges the commission to reconsider a legislative proposal once it has been the subject of a 'reasoned opinion' by one third of the national parliaments. the report notes that this yellow card has only once succeeded in persuading the commission to abandon a proposal. it's a very thin record. the report has the merit of denouncing this situation. but it is disappointing that it merely calls on the commission to engage in a dialogue with national parliaments and to improve its impact studies. a red card procedure should be created, allowing each member state to oppose a commission legislative proposal if it is detrimental to its vital interest. the right of veto would allow each state to enforce its sovereignty. it would be a first step towards replacing the european union with a europe of the nations.

in writing. - i voted against this bill. the report aims to substantially amend the definition of the principle of subsidiarity, currently laid down in article 5 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. the principle of subsidiarity is to limit the european union's intervention outside its exclusive competence and thus to preserve the prerogatives of sovereign states. the principle of proportionality is closely associated with it. in practice, the application of the principle of subsidiarity is lacking and the european commission has made many distortions of the principle. the appeals of national parliaments are largely illusory. the appeal procedure should therefore be strengthened by establishing a genuine red card mechanism for national parliaments.
