in writing. ‒ since 1992, the eu has developed the concept of 'policy coherence for development' (pcd). the aim of the cpd is to bring policies in this area closer together. it must also ensure that development policies remain favourable to the countries concerned. this report is based on the commission's fifth biannual report on the cpd. since becoming an mep, i have been denouncing the neoliberal logic of these policies and their harmful impact on local economies and populations, even to the point of preventing the sustainable development of some countries. it would be imperative that companies operating abroad ensure respect for human rights within their structures and take responsibility for violations. it is also recommended that development policies give priority to helping poor producers, promoting the diversity of the internal market of the countries concerned, reducing income gaps and promoting gender equality. finally, the report calls for the opening of legal pathways for migration and the improvement of reception of refugees. it supports a common asylum policy which is essential to overcome the current difficulties. without any illusions about the real impact of the report, i voted in favour of the report as a step in the right direction.

in writing. ‒ the new alliance for food security and nutrition in africa (nasan) has been the subject of much criticism since it came into force in 2012. it is a large public-private partnership of the g8, the african union, with an african agricultural development programme. a dozen african countries are involved, from ethiopia to côte d'ivoire and senegal. nearly 180 companies are participating in the programme for an investment of $8 billion. the tax, land and trade measures taken must provide a favourable environment for enterprises. but it repeats the destructive pattern imposed on asia in the 1970s (dependence on fertilisers, monoculture, export crops, etc.). this is why unsustainable farming is favoured, while smallholders are left behind. the report proposes to counterbalance these negative effects by stimulating family farming and local economies, and by fighting poverty and food insecurity. the report highlights the crucial issue of food sovereignty, and does not fail to point out that good agricultural and food policies in african countries reduce emigration. i voted in favour of this excellent report.

in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report concerns the new alliance for food security and nutrition (nasan), which was set up in 2012 under the auspices of the g8. the theoretical objective is to improve food security and nutrition in sub-saharan africa. while this objective is of course paramount, the means employed are more than questionable, as many ngos point out. nasan, for example, forces the african countries concerned to reduce the tax burden of partner companies, or worse, farmers to sign contracts with companies that force them to go into debt and take responsibility for bad harvests. there are no words to condemn such practices. the report is particularly useful because it is very critical of such practices. among other things, it contains false statements against the public-private partnership established by nasan and against the programme for helping multinational companies to develop their markets rather than local businesses and farmers. in short, the report denounces the methods of nasan and calls on the european union to remedy them. so i voted for it.
in writing. ‒ the international accounting standards board (iasb) aims to develop a set of accounting standards that are applicable worldwide. these standards are called international financial reporting standards (ifrs). in the recent financial crisis, certain standards were singled out. ifrss are based on principles, not rules. this gives accounting freedom of interpretation and makes it difficult to compare companies. ifrs also give an accounting view that is too favourable to investors. they tend to favour a short-term strategy which is detrimental to the markets. the report highlights these points and also criticises the iasb for a lack of progress in seeking transparency, preventing conflicts of interest or diversifying the experts involved. however, this report is too favourable to the generalisation of ifrs standards. if we accept the principle of common accounting standards, these standards remain questionable. the accounting regulations, which were previously the prerogative of the states, are now entrusted to an international organisation over which the states have little control. so i decided to abstain.

in writing. ‒ the international accounting standards board (iasb) aims to develop a set of accounting standards that are applicable worldwide, and thus to create a common language for financial reporting worldwide. these standards are called international financial reporting standards (ifrs). despite the relevant comments and recommendations, i abstained on this report because it is also a champion of the use of ifrs in a globalised economy. while we accept the principle of common accounting standards in order to facilitate the exchange of information, ifrs standards are highly questionable on a number of key points which may make them illegitimate. first, the concept of 'fair value' for the valuation of the company's assets gives a view which corresponds mainly to the interests of investors, but not necessarily to those of employees, customers or even the state. this notion leads to short-term strategies. ifrs are determined by institutions that threaten our sovereignty, since accounting regulation, which was previously the prerogative of the states, is now entrusted to an international, private and extra-community organization.

in writing. - i abstained on this report. international accounting standards (ifrs) have been imposed on companies in the european union since 2005. this is not entirely satisfactory: the choice of 'fair value' for the valuation of assets has been one of the causes of the instability of financial markets observed in recent years. other problems must be raised: the issue of off-balance-sheet accounts, the absence of a common methodology for the valuation of illiquid and impaired assets. finally, the impartiality of the iasb, the body which originated ifrs standards, is also questionable: dominated by large private companies, it leaves no room for representatives of small and medium-sized enterprises. we are therefore not criticising the desirability of harmonised accounting standards. however, our reservations about ifrs are too strong to support this report.

in writing. - i voted for it. the report put to the vote proposes the introduction of a code of good conduct and legal measures. it can thus protect small and medium-sized enterprises (smes), producers and traders who have suffered for years from unfair competition from the large retailers. these companies have changed the french production system profoundly and have almost completely monopolized distribution. in view of this, it is time to revalue the other food chains. i am in favour of this text, despite the fact that there is no denunciation of free trade agreements which erase trade frontiers.
in writing. ‒ the food chain links three important sectors of the european economy: agriculture, the agri-food industry and the distribution sector. they alone account for 7% of total employment. the major structural changes in this food chain have contributed in recent decades to creating economic imbalances in the individual trade relations between the various actors. this is why unfair trading practices (utps) in this chain are the subject of particular attention by the eu. while only about 20 member states have measures to combat pcd, the european commission still does not propose a solution. it merely encourages a flexible approach, leaving the best to private voluntary initiatives. the report stresses that european farmers and consumers must enjoy fair conditions of sale and purchase. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful organisms. i support these measures and therefore vote in favour.
in writing. - i voted for this text. this report aims to provide smes/tes with the tools to combat unfair commercial practices in the retail sector. however, the problem of funds, which is the opening of trade frontiers without any economic protectionism, is, as usual, completely avoided by this text. that reservation aside, we support this text which is in the interests of the agricultural community.
in writing. ‒ the report exposes unfair trading practices in the food sector. he cites as an example 'unfavourable negotiations with other actors in the food supply chain, for example during market closures and cuts in supermarkets', which forced producers to work at a loss. this phenomenon is also increasing because the increasing concentration of market power in a limited number of multinational groups tends to harm small and medium-sized producers. but if the report is positive, the options are weak. the report timidly calls for 'the most transparent retail pricing possible' so that prices in the food supply chain reflect the value added by primary producers. finally, it welcomed the commission's action in this area. i abstain in order not to prevent some small progress but i regret that maximum multiplier coefficients are not being put in place to stop the looting by the large retailers.

in writing. ‒ it is time to put an end to unfair trading practices in the food supply chain and that is why i voted in favour of this report, for which i was rapporteur for my political group. these unacceptable practices have very damaging consequences for the whole food supply chain, in particular for farmers and smes, as well as for the consumer. contractual freedom and the effective implementation of the applicable tools or legislation must be guaranteed to protect all actors in the chain, regardless of their geographical location. in particular, we call on the voluntary supply chain initiative to address its shortcomings, such as the under-representation of smes and farmers, the absence of sanctions for non-compliance, weaknesses in governance, and the inability to submit confidential complaints. we also encourage member states to set up specific public authorities or bodies at national level to combat such practices; in addition, those authorities should cooperate effectively with each other. the time has come to put an end to the doubts about the existence of such practices; we must now put an end to it.
in writing. ‒ the food supply chain has undergone major structural changes which have contributed to a situation characterised by highly variable levels of bargaining power and economic imbalances in individual trading relationships between actors in the chain. these imbalances are now reflected in recurrent unfair trading practices that weaken smaller players, such as producers. it is essential that the european commission addresses this problem through a legislative proposal that makes it possible to combat these unfair trading practices. to be effective, the response will have to be european, particularly in terms of adopting a common definition and standards. it will also have to take account of the particularly difficult situation of small players, particularly producers. the supply chain initiative, while a useful initiative, still has too many imperfections. for example, it has never been able to resolve a conflict between the various actors. it is therefore necessary to supplement it with binding measures, as this report calls for. it also states that such measures should include enforcement elements and dissuasive sanctions. i therefore supported this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this text, which calls on the european commission to take measures and tools at european level to combat unfair trading practices between companies. the problem of unfair competition is particularly acute in the food supply chain and has negative effects on the weakest link in the chain, in particular small producers and farmers. the report calls for the abusive practices of certain companies to be brought under control without delay in order to restore fair trading conditions. i supported this report because it also calls for the establishment of a framework legislation at union level, which is necessary to combat unfair trading practices and ensure that european farmers and consumers enjoy fair conditions of sale and purchase. this european framework legislation should not lower the level of protection already in force in some member states. the report also calls for greater transparency and access to more information in the supply chain, in particular to better inform consumers through product labelling.

in writing. ‒ i voted overall in favour of this text which talks at length about pesticides, indicating the need for farmers to become less dependent on these products and calling for a change in the regulatory framework. however, on behalf of the socialist and democratic group, i have called for great caution in regard to anything that comes out of genetic selection. agricultural research is now using new techniques for modifying living organisms: gene activation or deletion, recombination of the genome, assisted mutagenesis, etc. these new breeding techniques, known as nbt, are closely linked to seeds and raise legitimate concerns that they are reintroducing the debate on gmos. on the technical side, i wanted to distinguish between methods based on transgenesis (the insertion of a foreign gene into the genome), which i reject in the name of the precautionary principle, and methods based on endogenous improvement within the same species, which is the basis of agriculture and has been practised for centuries.

in writing. ‒ the report takes stock of the situation in agriculture: competition for land, scarcity of resources (water, air, etc.) and climate change. and to promote 'sustainable' agriculture in this context, the report encourages the development and adoption of 'precision' agricultural technologies, i.e. taking into account the variability of environments and conditions between different plots in order to optimise yields and investments. in fact, under the guise of reducing inputs (because they are better used), this is a new race for equipment requiring expensive technologies and therefore a large amount of debt on the part of farmers. to guarantee genetic diversity, rather than opposing the patenting of living things, the text hypocritically proposes 'a better dialogue between gene banks, private and public plant research, breeders, end users'. the text does, however, allow some leeway for the organic model: for example, it admits that 'biocontrols (methods of crop protection based on the use of living organisms or natural substances) could limit the use of traditional pesticides and contribute to a better resilience of plants'. but the account isn't there. and, in the end, this report reflects the absolute lack of vision for the future of agriculture in europe. i vote against it.

in writing. ‒ according to the food and agriculture organization of the united nations (fao), the world's food supply will need to increase by 60% by 2050. to achieve this, the report proposes to encourage 'innovation' in agriculture. the report is critical of the current agricultural model. it criticizes the use of pesticides and inputs, promotes organic farming and even agroforestry. it also takes food sovereignty issues into account by calling for protein independence in the eu. but it is also committed to ensuring 'the continuous development of innovative plant breeding techniques'. behind this barbaric terminology lies the possibility for pharmaceutical companies to manipulate the genetic material of plants to claim intellectual property. in other words, it allows gmos. the new techniques, new varieties or new machinery that this report is touting will have the first consequence of increasing farmers' dependence on multinational plant protection companies and banks. this will increase the gap between large agro-industrial producers and small farmers. i am voting against this text, which clearly does not address the issues of the new agriculture that has become necessary (environment, employment, culture, landscape, etc.).
in writing. ‒ despite the clear evidence, the conclusions are ideological and worrying in areas as varied as the cap, strategy 2020, the digital single market, gmos, icts, rpas. i therefore voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report contains far too many inadmissible elements. it opens the door to changes we do not want, for example on gmos. the few interesting findings are drowned in a disturbing ultra-liberal tide. i am voting against this text.
in writing. ‒ as in all sectors, innovation in agriculture is essential to meet the new challenges that are emerging: increasing world population, decreasing arable land... this report highlights the role of innovation in economic and environmental sustainability in agricultural production. that's why i voted for it.
in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report contains far too many inadmissible elements. it opens the door to changes we do not want, for example on gmos. the few interesting findings are drowned in a disturbing ultra-liberal tide. i am voting against this text.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which emphasises innovation as a factor of economic and environmental sustainability in agricultural production. this text sets out various proposals to facilitate access for our farmers to the various new production techniques, whether on traditional, small-scale farms or in areas facing geographical or natural handicaps, such as mountain areas or overseas.
in writing. ‒ we are facing three challenges to which agricultural innovation can provide solutions: a food challenge, with the prospect of having to feed 9.1 billion people by 2050, an environmental challenge, due to the degradation and depletion of natural resources, and finally a climate challenge, linked to climate change at work and the risks it entails. meeting these challenges requires redefining the objectives of the common agricultural policy (cap) and facilitating funding for agricultural innovation. the range of possible innovations is wide, from technological innovations (digital, robotics), to innovations in terms of agricultural practices (better protection and exploitation of resources), or in terms of social organisation (developing the circular economy, for example). the stakes are twofold. while the redefinition of cap objectives must provide solutions to the challenges facing agriculture, it must also ensure that it does not leave farmers alone in the face of crises in their sector, such as in milk or pig farming. innovation must be used to develop agricultural potential, sustainability and food security.
in writing. ‒ the very title of this report says a lot about the ideological garbage it is. it contains a great number of ideas, measures and new regulatory avenues, which i regularly combat:- excessive productivism;- exaltation of the cap, the europe 2020 strategy and the digital single market;- dogmatic defence of ict, even though it is not always effective (especially in the establishment of cadastral registers by gps, which are often approximate);- promotion of a global harmonisation of the european market through, in particular, the use and exchange of personal data;- desire to create jobs, but an incentive for the commission to push for ever more automation of tasks;- desire to introduce, via the commission, a single european legislation for drones and rasps. in particular, mr huitema distills throughout his report his promotion of gmos and strongly challenges the existing legislation in europe on the subject. 'bio-stimulants', 'biocontrols' and 'biological control mechanisms' are therefore marketed as essential tools for 21st century agriculture. this own-initiative report contains far too many inadmissible elements. it opens the door to changes i don't want. the few interesting findings are drowned in a disturbing ultra-liberal tide. i vote against it.
in writing. ‒ according to the food and agriculture organisation of the united nations, the world population will reach 9.1 billion by 2050; as a result, the food supply will have to be increased by 60%. this is an opportunity that the european agri-food industry will no doubt seize. to encourage this, the report supports a widespread use of information and communication technologies (ict) to improve 'competitiveness and innovation'. the usual european leitmotifs with the hoped-for result of higher productivity and incomes, and even job creation. however, it is useful to recall the consequences of the 'green revolution' of the 1930s and 1960s. during this period, other new technologies were introduced with known negative effects on small farmers, the environment and food sovereignty. we are paying the price today. in addition, this report risks opening the door to gmos, and the solutions advocated, which are based mainly on technology and machines, cannot be the right ones. instead, we must move towards a change of system, towards a way of producing that is agro-ecological and that defends small farmers. i therefore voted against without hesitation.

of the parliament, mr president, i am really pleased to present before you today a revised eu blue card proposal and an eu action plan on integration. from the very beginning, this house has valued the importance of having sound and forward-looking legal migration policies, which are the other important side of the coin of managing migration comprehensively and in an effective way. but legal migration goes beyond migration and mobility as such. it plays an important role in strengthening the eu’s competitiveness and it can address demographic challenges and labour shortages. while, on the one hand, we will need to continue investing in the skills of our existing workforce and addressing unemployment, the rapid ageing of the population in the european union will require us to attract skills from abroad to address shortages in specific sectors. i will give you two examples. in the ict sector we need more than 100 000 highly skilled professionals per year. in the health sector there will be around one million unfilled highly skilled vacancies by 2020. even if we upskill our labour force, this takes time. besides that, we will still need more people to fill the shortages. let me also state another fact, which i know is difficult to hear in the current context: european societies are and will continue to become increasingly diverse. today there are 20 million non-eu nationals residing in the european union – around 4% of its total population. the key element here is not to fight this reality but to embrace it and turn it into an advantage by ensuring the successful integration of migrants – including, of course, refugees – into the host societies as soon as possible, therefore maximising the benefits of immigration. today’s proposals address all these issues. on the blue card, the european union is increasingly competing with the growing number of other destinations for the same global pool of talent. we want to become more attractive than countries such as australia, canada and the united states of america. therefore, the eu needs to establish a more efficient, transparent and simpler scheme for attracting highly skilled workers. this will bring substantial benefits to the european union in terms of innovation, transfer of technology and increased investment flows. this will enhance the european union’s competitiveness and help create new jobs. in fact, the new blue card scheme would bring an estimated post-dip annual economic impact of between eur 1.4 billion to eur 6.2 billion from additional highly skilled workers coming to the european union to take up jobs. right now, the existing blue card is unattractive, unknown and fragmented. so, how can we change? how can we remedy these shortcomings? today’s proposal aims at establishing an ambitious europe-wide scheme. it will be easier to qualify for the eu blue card. the scheme is also made more accessible if you have graduated recently or work in a shortage occupation. the eu blue card is also made accessible to highly skilled beneficiaries of international protection. this will allow them to make full use of their potential and skills and support their integration. the blue card can be obtained faster because the maximum processing time is shorter. the new proposal also provides for enhanced rights in terms of intra-eu mobility, access to employment and long-term residence, and for family members. on the action plan on integration, we are not starting from scratch on integration but we should learn from the past when looking at the future. if we look at integration outcomes across the european union, third country nationals continue to face barriers in the education systems or the labour market. they are more at risk of poverty or social exclusion. the recent inflow of third country nationals to europe, and in particular of refugees, represents an additional challenge but is also an opportunity and we have to seize this window of opportunity. it is therefore high time to investment more on integration if we want to ensure that all third country nationals can fully contribute to our economies and societies. i want to be very clear: the cost of non-integration in the longer-term will be higher than the cost of investing today in effective integration policies. on the other hand, if we succeed in making integration a success story, this will be highly beneficial, both for the host countries and for the migrants themselves. effective integration also entails an understanding and subscribing to eu fundamental rights and values. this is an essential element of living and participating in the european union, and we should not shy away from addressing this question when we define what it means to live in and belong to europe. now, while we fully recognise that integration policies are made and done at national, and particularly at regional and local levels, it is also true that those levels across the european union are experiencing the same challenges. so the european union has a role to play in supporting all stakeholders in this process in coordinating and in helping structurally and financially. the action plan adopted today offers a comprehensive framework to support member states’ efforts in developing and strengthening their integration policies. it targets all third country nationals in the european union while including several actions that address the specific challenges faced by refugees. the key areas of action that we have identified are: firstly, support to third country nationals, but also the communities that welcome them at the earliest possible moment in the migration process through pre-departure and pre-arrival measures. secondly, education and training. thirdly, integration of third country nationals into the labour market and into vocational training. fourthly, facilitating access to basic services such as adequate and affordable housing and health. fifthly, and finally, the action plan also proposes to strengthen the coordination between the various actors working on integration at national, regional and local level and proposes a more strategic approach towards the use of eu funds for integration, not only asylum, migration and integration funds but also the european social fund and other relevant eu funds. honourable members of the parliament, i look forward to hearing your comments on our proposals today but most importantly, i count on you to help us turn them into reality as soon as possible. it was one and a half years ago that i was committed to bring this proposal here today and i am more than happy to do so.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, thank you very much for allowing me to intervene in the debate. i think it is better to be more interactive in this way. i have just a few comments on the interventions we have heard so far. it is very important for the eib to remain a triple-a bank, because triple-a status has a direct connection to the financing power the eib has. but i fully agree with members who have said that the eib should take more risk, and for this reason we have established the efsi. it enables the eib to finance projects which are seen as more risky and is worth eur 63 billion. this is what the eib is doing at the moment. the eib has done an excellent job. apart from adding finance to risky projects, it has upgraded its presence in many of our member states, including greece, in order to help the greek authorities, and the private sector especially, to benefit from efsi and benefit from other financial instruments of the eib. the eib has done its share very, very well. one issue i want to raise in the debate – and i want to raise awareness amongst meps on this issue – is that it is also possible to combine structural funds with efsi. we already have a very good example of this kind of financing in northern france where the nord-pas-de-calais region has organised an investment platform which aims to gather together a large number of smes and start—ups, especially in the digital field. they will use private capital, regional money and efsi funds in order to provide risk financing for those companies. you can find this example on the website. this is a model which could be copied in the other countries, especially the cohesion countries. there we need the help of meps, because you know efsi funds and you know the regions. efsi is a demand—driven fund. i am happy that we have one genuine circular economic project which has got financing from efsi, but i am dissatisfied that there is only one. so, again, we have to raise awareness amongst circular economy players and investors that efsi can really provide something which the market cannot provide, or does not provide, at the moment. efsi is a perfect instrument for the circular economy, for new innovation and new technology investments, which for some reason cannot get full financing from the market. there again, the role of meps is crucial. the eib does not create projects, it only finances them, and that is why we have to raise awareness amongst investors, and also amongst the regions and cities to use efsi for new innovations. i want to raise one issue. we are following very closely what is going on in our member states in terms of efsi activities and related things. i have very good information on the activities of meps. so far only a handful of meps have organised efsi events in their regions or member states. a very good example of these kinds of activities was last week, when i had a chance to visit mr pittella’s and mr gualtieri’s event, where southern italian regional leaders came together. we were talking about opportunities to use efsi for southern italian purposes. also, ms spyraki has organised events in greece, ms paunova in bulgaria, and mr guoga in lithuania. this is exactly what we need at the moment. we need to raise awareness of what efsi can do and what efsi has done in other countries in order to make it possible to use efsi in a more efficient way. if you want to see the projects which have already been signed, you can find all the projects on the internet. it is very good to look at them and pass the message on to the other regions about what the others have already done. efsi will not solve all the problems in europe. in the best case, it can provide financing or it can help to get investments worth eur 315 billion euros. this is only one third of what is needed. that is why the other parts of the investment plans are even more important than efsi. it is easier to talk about money when we are talking about eur 315 billion, or what efsi has already financed, but the rest of the plan is even more important. that is why i expect co—legislators to be as fast when implementing, or when approving, single market—related proposals as we were when we approved efsi legislation. it took only six months to push efsi through the parliament and the council. why should we wait longer when dealing with, for instance, a waste legislation proposal or digital single market-related proposals? so the internal market-side of the plan is even more important than efsi, even though efsi is very much needed.
madam president, the juncker fund is perhaps the european commission's flagship initiative. it aims to fill the investment gap that europe has suffered for a decade. the first projects financed are numerous and encouraging, but it is still too early to draw up a reliable balance sheet and, in this respect, mr katainen, you will have to dispel three doubts. the first doubt concerns the requirement of additionality of the fund, i.e. its added value. we will have to show that without the juncker fund, the projects in question would not have been financed. the second doubt concerns the temptation to which some public investors might succumb to deconsolidate capital expenditure and the corresponding debt, in order to make the presentation of public accounts visually lighter. the third doubt concerns the risk of replacing market operators with the european investment bank, which has the competitive advantage of the guarantee of the fund. the fund is stimulating, but we must bear in mind that the obstacles to investment are still very much in place. firstly, in the market sector, investment is conditioned by competitiveness. that is, if countries that are slow to reform cannot expect a miracle. beyond the member states, the union has its own brakes, particularly when the monetary environment is under question. investors are afraid of uncertainty. there is an urgent need to settle the uk referendum, to draw the consequences and to reform the governance of the euro area to make it more efficient and more democratic. finally, the commitment of operators depends on the predictability and stability of the market rules. in many areas, the single market is fragmented by national regulations, by local competition authorities. there is also an urgent need to complete the single market, to speed up the convergence of tax and social legislation, in short, to make the euro area and the european union an optimal economic area. the commission is clearly pleased with the initial results of the juncker fund and is considering making it permanent. financial engineering can increase volumes tenfold. the guarantee must, however, be called in in the form of a clear and madam president, mr vice-president, we must make the investment plan a success, so let us give ourselves the means to make it a success. you said earlier that the efsi is there to finance what the market cannot finance. but that's where the real work begins. doubts are mounting as to the additionality of the system. the eib's choices do not seem any riskier than before and our objectives concerning employment, cohesion and the energy transition are being neglected. we must correct the system as quickly as possible so that it can help projects other than those with a high level of profitability and which could probably have been financed by the market. one of the corrections which i think is necessary is to abandon the search for the highest multiplier effect, which mechanically implies that the most profitable projects are retained and that the most risky but often most structural projects are rejected at the same time. it is not a question of throwing the baby out with the bath water, but of adapting the system so that it can respond to projects with a low multiplier effect and less profitable, but - as i said - more structural, responding in particular to the priorities of energy transition, cohesion and employment.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, let me first thank the rapporteur, mrs de sarnez, and the committee on international trade (inta), for the valuable work on this report. as we all know, tunisia faces enormous political economic challenges, and that is the reason why the commission made its proposal for a macro—financial assistance operation in that country. tunisia is confronted with the consequences of the terrorist attacks of 2015. the result is that its vital tourism sector, in particular, has been seriously affected and foreign investments have sharply declined. these developments have led to falling growth rates and foreign currency reserves. this shows that the situation is very acute, and tunisia needs international financial systems in order to stabilise and further political transition started during the arab spring of 2011. international bilateral donors, led by the imf, have clearly expressed their willingness to support tunisia, now and in the near future. the commission can and should contribute to these renewed financial support efforts and we propose to do so by providing a new macro-financial assistance (mfa) of eur 500 million which builds on the previous mfa operation of eur 300 million. it is foreseen that this new assistance, which is the largest mfa ever given to a country of the southern neighbourhood, will be disbursed in three tranches over the next two years. this exceptional assistance effort must also be seen against the background of the courageous efforts and significant progress that tunisia has been making in recent years to establish a fully—fledged democratic system, despite the difficult regional and security environment. of course, the new mfa operation will be subject to the fulfilment of a number of economic policy conditions. indeed, tunisia must satisfactorily implement the new imf programme and fulfil economic and financial policy conditions to be agreed between the eu and tunisia in a memorandum of understanding. potential policy measures could cover areas such as public finance management, fiscal reforms, strengthening the social safety net, labour market reforms and measures to support the recovery of the tourism sector, as well as in trade and investment. i would like to stress that timing is of the essence here. tunisia requires the micro-financial assistance to cover its large external financing needs for 2016 and 2017, so a swift adoption of the current proposal by co-legislators, under the ordinary legislative procedure is very important. therefore, i am pleased that the inta committee has approved the commission proposal without amendment. i am also pleased that the council in the letter from coreper, has expressed its commitment to adopting a commission proposal without amendments, subject to the same outcome at today’s plenary vote. thank you for your attention and i look forward to having a fruitful debate.

in writing. ‒ this agreement is an extension of the 1996 information technology agreement, following the wto ministerial conference in nairobi in december 2012, where wto members reached a landmark agreement to eliminate tariffs on 201 information technology products. the agreement also includes a commitment to work towards the elimination of non-tariff barriers in this sector and to keep the list of products covered open so that it can be extended in line with future technological developments. this type of extension of an existing agreement allows many products to be brought back into the free trade circuit, which is catastrophic for the french economy; i therefore voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this draft council decision on the conclusion, on behalf of the european union, of an agreement in the form of a declaration on the expansion of trade in information technology products (itp). the agreement aims to extend the 1996 agreement on information technology and will remove virtually all customs duties on these products by 2019. apart from the great danger of this measure, which will lead to unbridled competition in our information technology industry (against giants such as china, taiwan and south korea), i would like to stress that once again this unbridled free trade programme was prepared by the large multinationals meeting in nairobi on 16 december. the wto director himself admitted that this agreement was historic. this will put at risk all our smes working in the field of gps navigation systems, imaging equipment and telecommunications satellites. once again, the big groups, with the complicity of our ruling elites, are agreeing to eliminate all measures to protect the interests of the people.
in writing. ‒ this agreement is an extension of the 1996 agreement on information technologies. under the agreement, by 2019, tariffs on almost all these products will be zero for the 82 participating countries. the wto director-general said: "this agreement is the first major tariff reduction agreement in the wto since 1996". it also includes a commitment to work towards the elimination of non-tariff barriers and to leave the list of products covered open for consideration in order to determine whether further enlargement will be necessary to take account of future technological developments. this new free trade agreement further increases the pressure of global competition in this sector, with the future consequence of large job losses in eu countries. it increases the dependence of our countries on those with low labour costs in this very strategic area. for these reasons, i voted against.
in writing. ‒ the text aims to remove customs duties on almost all information technology products by 2019. on 16 december, the wto ministerial conference was held in nairobi, during which wto members drew up a timetable for implementing the elimination of customs duties on 201 information technology products, whose trade is estimated at eur 1 300 billion a year. the agreement covers next-generation semiconductors, gps navigation systems, machine tools used in the manufacture of printed circuit boards, telecommunications satellites and touchscreens. i have of course opposed this agreement, which includes a section on the removal of non-tariff barriers. on the contrary, we should guard against the savage globalisation which has been responsible for the deindustrialisation of the western countries since the early 1980s. this free trade agreement, like the previous ones, will contribute to the unfair international competition that our companies face. this is why any removal of tariff and non-tariff barriers must be reciprocal and conditional on compliance with anti-dumping laws.
in writing. i supported the conclusion of an agreement in the form of a declaration on the expansion of trade in information technology products (itp). the agreement provides for the elimination of customs duties on more than 200 information technology products. it will lower prices for consumers, but also for producers who depend on imported components.
in writing. ‒ this report follows the historic agreement reached on 16 december 2015 at the world trade organisation in nairobi, which provides for the elimination of customs duties on more than 200 information technology products, such as gps navigation systems, medical products, telecommunications satellites and touch screens. i support the approval of this agreement, which will see all imports of communications technology products benefit from a total elimination of customs duties by 2019. this will provide a real stimulus to growth by promoting global trade and eu exports will benefit greatly.
in writing. ‒ on 16 december, at the wto ministerial conference in nairobi, wto members representing major exporters of information technology products agreed on a timetable for implementing a landmark agreement. the aim of the agreement is to eliminate customs duties on 201 information technology products, with an estimated $1.3 trillion in trade per year. the products covered by the agreement are next-generation semiconductors, gps navigation systems, medical products such as magnetic resonance imaging equipment, machine tools used in the manufacture of printed circuit boards, telecommunications satellites and touch screens. the agreement also includes a commitment to work towards the elimination of non-tariff barriers, by allowing many products to be integrated into the free trade system in a non-transparent way. i therefore voted against this text.

in writing. ‒ the text focuses on the agreement currently being prepared, which aims to extend the 1996 agreement on information and communication technologies. under the auspices of the world trade organisation (wto), the 82 participants (the united states, russia, japan, korea, china, the european union, etc.) entered into negotiations in 2012 with the aim of reducing tariffs on almost all information products to zero by 2019. the agreement covers 201 products (new generation semiconductors, gps navigation systems, medical products with imaging equipment, etc.). this historic agreement will eventually remove non-tariff barriers to information technology, allowing major global producers such as asian countries to invade our markets without resistance or opposition. i voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ the revision of the agreement on the expansion of trade in information technology products (ati-2), concluded within the wto on 16 december 2015, provides for the gradual elimination of customs duties on 201 information technology products. this includes computers, telephones, touch screens, gps navigation equipment, medical devices such as mri or ultrasonic scanning diagnostic devices, but also inputs, and other components and machines. trade in these products is valued at $1.3 trillion a year, or about 10% of world trade in goods. this agreement not only has a significant potential to stimulate growth but also to increase global trade in high-tech products. it also represents a significant market expansion opportunity for many european industrialists, particularly french ones. rapid ratification of the agreement will certainly send a positive signal and help to enhance the wto's responsiveness to adapting the regulation of world trade to the rapidly changing nature of information technology products. i therefore vote in favour of this recommendation.

in writing. ‒ the quisthoudt-rowohl report proposed that a multilateral agreement be concluded on trade in information technology products (itp), a sector in which the union and france are major players at world level. the aim is to phase out customs duties on 201 information technology products (computers, telephones, but also gps, mri devices, etc.), representing around 10% of world trade in goods. the agreement, which involves 82 countries, should be welcomed as an important step towards relaunching the multilateral system, which by definition has more safeguards than bilateral mega-trade agreements (ttip, ceta) or plurilateral ones (tisa). i have supported this multilateral agreement in particular because it addresses france's aggressive interests in trade in high value-added goods, while providing temporary protection for its sensitive technological products, such as electric meters, optical lenses or optical fibres. the challenge now is to make these new markets flourish, to the benefit of french and european workers and consumers.
in writing. ‒ the first information technology agreement (ita) was adopted at the singapore ministerial conference in december 1996 and entered into force in 1997. the agreement provides for each of the 21 participants to eliminate customs duties on all the information technology products covered. these include more than 200 products: computers, telephones, but also inputs, components and machines used in the manufacture of information technology products. the number of products concerned is now being extended to include next-generation semiconductors, gps navigation systems, touch screens and even medical products such as magnetic resonance imaging diagnostic devices. the resolution before us approves this proposal. with this agreement, the european information technology industries will be subject to increased competition and employees to social dumping. i vote against it.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which gives the european parliament's approval to the agreement to extend the information technology agreement (ita). this agreement was concluded within the wto on 16 december at the wto ministerial conference in nairobi by 53 wto members (the ati now has 82 participating countries). the agreement will eliminate customs duties on 201 information technology products, whose trade is estimated at more than €1 trillion a year. annual trade in these products accounts for about 10% of total world trade. according to the agreement, approximately 65% of tariff lines will be completely eliminated by 1 july 2016. by 2019, almost all imports of the products concerned will benefit from duty-free access. the products covered by the agreement include next-generation semiconductors, gps navigation systems, telecommunications satellites and touchscreens. finally, it should be noted that the union has negotiated a phasing-out of the reductions over a longer period for certain products considered sensitive.

in writing. ‒ this report concerns the 1996 hns convention drawn up under the auspices of the international maritime organisation, the 2010 protocol amending it and the 2010 hns convention consolidating the two texts mentioned above. the convention establishes the objective liability of the owner of a ship carrying harmful or potentially dangerous substances for damage resulting from an incident at sea during such transport, provides for limited exceptions to this liability, which is accompanied by the obligation to take out insurance or other financial security to cover his liability for damage covered by the convention, establishes a specific compensation fund to compensate any person who has suffered damage in connection with the carriage of harmful substances by sea where the owner of the ship concerned or his insurer is not liable for the amount of the reparations. the report considers that, in order to ensure uniform application of the rules on liability and redress for such accidents, an international regime is more appropriate than regional solutions, given the global nature of the maritime freight transport activity. that is why i voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ this report supports the ratification of the 2010 protocol to the international convention on hazardous and noxious substances, as regards aspects related to judicial cooperation in civil matters. the convention establishes the liability of the owner of a vessel carrying harmful substances in the event of damage resulting from an accident at sea. it provides for limited exceptions to this liability, which is accompanied by the obligation to take out insurance. finally, it established a specific fund to cover the full amount of loss and damage suffered by an individual who could not have been fully compensated by the owner of the vessel or by his insurer. i believe that a global approach is better suited than regional solutions, given the global nature of the maritime sector and its cross-border implications. that is why i voted for this text.
in writing. ‒ under the auspices of the international maritime organisation (imo), the 1996 hns (hazardous and noxious substances) convention was amended by the 2010 protocol. in the event of damage resulting from an incident during the transport of harmful or potentially dangerous substances, the convention establishes the objective liability of the ship owner, with limited exceptions accompanied by the obligation to take out insurance. the agreement also establishes a compensation fund for those who have not been able to obtain satisfactory reparation for the damage. i supported this text, which says that the uniform application of international rules on liability and compensation for such accidents is better suited than regional solutions.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of ratifying and acceding to the 2010 protocol to the international convention on hazardous and noxious substances, as regards aspects relating to judicial cooperation in civil matters. the convention establishes the objective liability of the owner of a ship carrying harmful or potentially dangerous substances in the event of damage resulting from an incident at sea during such transport. it provides for limited exceptions to this liability, which is accompanied by the obligation to take out insurance or other financial guarantee to cover one's liability in the event of damage. it establishes a specific compensation fund to compensate any person who has suffered damage in connection with the carriage of harmful and potentially dangerous substances by sea where he has been unable to obtain full and adequate compensation for the damage from the ship owner and his insurer. the report rightly considers that, in order to ensure uniform application of the rules on liability and redress for such accidents, an international regime is better suited than regional solutions, given the global nature of the maritime sector and its cross-border implications.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the release of emergency macro-financial assistance (mfa) of eur 500 million to tunisia. the tunisian economy is in serious trouble: unemployment, especially among young people, is at an all-time high and regional inequalities are growing dangerously. the economic challenges facing tunisia have been significantly exacerbated by terrorist attacks targeting the tourism and transport sectors. but the amf is only a loan, which tunisia will have to repay. the european union must look beyond this. in conjunction with the international community, it must work to reduce tunisia's debt and unblock the process of repatriating assets embezzled by the ben ali regime - in this case partly held in european banks. otherwise, this new amf will not serve its purpose.

in writing. ‒ taxes must be paid where profits are made! this is what is advocated in the report by my socialist colleague, mr hugues bayet, who also proposes new rules to combat tax evasion. the report also gives the go-ahead for the establishment of a committee of inquiry into the panama papers. there is a legitimate exasperation among our citizens, who realise that one of the great principles of our democracies - equality before tax - is being flouted and undermined by a number of practices such as tax optimisation, which allow many multinationals to pay ridiculously low taxes, and moreover in countries where they have no real economic activity. we must put an end to it once and for all!
in writing. ‒ the commission proposes a series of measures in a directive to combat tax evasion by groups of companies. after those on the automatic exchange of rescripts, this directive is central because it tackles the most common and costly mechanisms for public finances, at the heart of avoidance schemes. the text proposes six regulatory points: capping the deductibility of interest, taxing the exit of latent capital gains, introducing switch over clauses, a general anti-abuse clause, rules for the transfer of profits from parent companies to foreign companies under control and less taxed, hybrid schemes generating non-taxation. it should also be noted that the text provides a legal definition of tax havens, stable establishments, patent boxes and other key concepts in the fight against aggressive optimisation. the bayet report modifies some sensitive points of the commission proposal: for example, it doubles the thresholds for deductibility of excess interest and introduces exemptions for financial companies or public investors. as france is one of the least welcoming countries in the eu in tax matters, we have more to gain from restrictive legislation than the other way around. so i voted for it.

in writing. ‒ the commission presented in january 2016 a series of measures to combat tax evasion. this directive tackles the most common and costly mechanisms for public finances by proposing several regulatory points, such as an anti-abuse clause and by formulating a legal definition of the different key concepts in the fight against fiscal optimisation. the report made some changes to the commission's draft, for example by introducing various exemptions for financial companies. however, the european parliament is not a co-legislator here: as with all taxation matters, the council will retain the last word. i voted in favour of this report in order to support these advances which are in the interest of european public finances in general and french public finances in particular, france being one of the least tax-friendly countries in the eu.
in writing. ‒ this directive is crucial and proposes in particular six regulatory points: the cap on the deductibility of interest, the exit tax, the introduction of switch over clauses (taxation with a tax credit for foreign flows already taxed but at a significantly lower rate), a general anti-abuse clause, rules for the shifting of profits from parent companies to foreign companies under control and less taxed, and the case of hybrid schemes generating non-taxation. this bayet report modified some sensitive points in relation to the commission's proposal concerning the thresholds for deductibility of excess interest or the period for carrying forward excess ebitda (too favourable to multinationals). i would remind you that france is one of the least tax-friendly countries in the eu and that this legislation is in the direction of our national public finances but also in the sense that we have more to gain from the legislation presented than from a status quo. i therefore voted in favour.

in writing. tax must be paid where profits are made: it is in keeping with this principle that i voted for this report which aims to close loopholes used by fraudulent companies and includes legally binding measures to block the most common methods used by companies to avoid paying taxes. the text thus provides for a precise and binding definition of the conditions which certify that a multinational is well established in a country. it includes the establishment of a strict, common 28 member state blacklist of tax havens and countries that distort competition by means of favourable tax conditions, including those located in the union. it proposes to cap interest deductions at 20% and up to €2 million, an ambitious and more balanced approach than the commission's proposal, which prevents multinationals from artificially inflating the number of loans they take out. finally, the use of patent filing (which artificially reduces the amount of profits) is to be restricted by clarifying the definition of investment in research and development. this is a real step forward and deserves support.

in writing. ‒ this text constitutes parliament's negotiating position on the proposal for a directive laying down rules to combat tax evasion practices which have a direct impact on the functioning of the internal market. the report contains many steps to combat these practices, including: - paying taxes where companies make their profits, through the precise and mandatory definition of the conditions that certify that a multinational is well established in a country; - the establishment of a strict and common blacklist of tax havens for the 28 member states, including those in the union; - the cap on interest deductions at 20% and up to €2 million, which prevents multinationals from artificially inflating the number of loans they take out; - the launch of a much-needed debate on a european-wide corporate tax rate, to eliminate the risk of tax competition. i support the implementation of these measures and therefore vote in favour of this text.
in writing. - i voted for this text. this atad directive is central because it tackles the most common and costly mechanisms for public finances, at the heart of avoidance schemes. it proposes six regulatory points: the cap on the deductibility of interest, taxation on the exit of latent capital gains (exit tax), the introduction of switch over clauses (taxation with a tax credit for foreign flows already taxed but at a significantly lower rate), a general anti-abuse clause, rules for the shifting of profits from parent companies to foreign companies under control and less taxed, and the case of hybrid schemes generating non-taxation. the text also provides a legal definition of tax havens, stable establishments, patent boxes and other key concepts in the fight against aggressive optimisation. we support this text because france is one of the least tax-friendly countries in the eu and we have more to gain from stricter legislation in the field of tax optimisation than from the status quo. the council will have the final say on taxation. the ministers of the 28 member states have not yet reached agreement, partly because of the opposition of the netherlands and ireland.
in writing. ‒ the european union is letting €1 trillion evaporate in tax avoidance and optimisation. this situation is maintaining a crisis of public revenue and is blamed on inequality in taxation between taxpayers - in particular between smes and households on the one hand, and large groups on the other. the bayet report, which amends the commission's proposal for an anti-tax evasion directive, contains the first serious measures that have been proposed for a long time to restore tax fairness and prevent white collar crime. in particular, for corporate income that returns to europe, the so-called 'switch-over' clause ensures that flows into the eu have been taxed at a rate that is not unfair. this clause has been cleverly supplemented by our rapporteur, mr bayet, to apply a common criterion to the whole of the european union. for outflows from europe, the measure of taxation on the exit of profits leaving the union completes the scheme. we have long forgotten, in focusing on double taxation, that there was also massive double non-taxation. these measures, and many others, have my full support, and i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the european commission, which has been forced to act following the luxleaks revelations, now wants minimum tax harmonisation. every year, tax evasion and avoidance strategies by multinational companies cost european states 1 billion in lost revenue. the commission is proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the context of the directive on the protection of consumers. parliament also wants to tax profit transfers to subsidiaries in countries where corporation tax is below 15%. while the text does not call into question the overall system of financial arrangements and tax havens allowing tax evasion, it proposes to limit the most visible abuses. i'm abstaining to encourage these measures.
in writing. ‒ the bayet report modified some sensitive points in relation to the commission's initial draft (thresholds for the deductibility of excess interest, the period for carrying forward excess ebitda, exemptions for financial companies or for public investments). the european parliament is not a co-legislator here, the council will have the last word. this regulation is an opportunity for france, which is one of the least tax-friendly countries in the eu. i think it is appropriate to support developments which will be beneficial to our national public finances. i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ in january 2016, the commission presented a set of measures in a directive to combat tax evasion by groups of companies. after those on the automatic exchange of rescripts or country-by-country reporting, this directive (called atad) is central because it tackles the most common and costly mechanisms for public finances, at the heart of avoidance schemes. on the appropriateness of this regulation, it should be recalled that france is one of the least tax-friendly countries in the eu and that we have more to gain from stricter legislation in the field of tax optimisation than in a status quo. our philosophy would certainly be that a french government should impose this on its partners, but the chances of success in bilateral relations with the economically liberal political majorities we know are low, as the present situation shows. it seems appropriate to continue along this line and to support these advances which will be in the interest of national public finances. i vote for it.
in writing. ‒ this text allows for progress which will be in the interest of national public finances, particularly french public finances. i therefore vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this text, which aims to neutralise tax avoidance techniques through six measures. this directive is part of the 'anti-tax avoidance' package which also includes a recommendation on tax conventions, a revision of the directive on administrative cooperation, a communication on an external strategy for effective taxation. the commission estimates that tax fraud and tax avoidance cost up to €1 trillion each year. we must therefore do everything we can to combat this phenomenon.
in writing. ‒ this text allows for progress which will be in the interest of national public finances, particularly french public finances. i therefore vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on the proposal for a directive laying down rules to combat tax evasion practices which have a direct impact on the functioning of the european internal market. the text, which has its origins in the action plan for fair and efficient business taxation presented by the european commission in june 2015, aims to adopt a strong and coherent approach at european level to combat abusive tax practices. this will include the implementation of the anti-tax avoidance directive in all member states, enhanced administrative cooperation between countries on taxation of multinationals and an external strategy for effective taxation to promote good tax governance worldwide.
in writing. ‒ the european union's policy of taking action to combat tax fraud and evasion is both a social justice imperative and an economic necessity for public authorities. this ambitious text is part of this policy. it is based on the principle that taxes should be paid where profits are made and includes legally binding measures to block the most common methods used by companies, or even member states, to minimise the taxes owed. it also proposes common definitions of terms which have hitherto remained open to interpretation, such as 'permanent establishment', 'tax havens' or 'mailbox companies'. while we welcome the progress made, we regret that this text falls under the consultation procedure, thus limiting the role that meps can play in this area. however, parliament strengthened the original proposal, notably with regard to the 'switch-over' clause (revenue taxed in a country outside the eu and then transferred to a member state of the union, often exempt from taxation to avoid double taxation). in accordance with the political lines presented, i voted in favour of this text.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which aims to establish new rules to combat tax evasion. after the swissleaks, luxleaks and panama papers scandals, which revealed the scale of tax evasion practices at european and global level, we must act to ensure that tax is paid where the profit is made. the philosophy of this report is to make five important advances: a precise and mandatory definition of the conditions that certify that a multinational is well established in a country in order to ensure that it pays its taxes there; the cap on interest deductions at 20% up to eur 2 million, the 'switch-over' clause allowing the regulation of controlled foreign companies; an ambitious 'taxation at the exit' of profits to reduce double non-taxation; limiting the use of patent filing (which artificially reduces the amount of profits) through a clarification of the definition of investment in research and development. these advances must help to restore equality in taxation, a principle which is at the heart of our democracies.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this text on the fight against tax evasion. this is a major blow to our economy and cannot be tolerated. as the report points out, the tax secrecy of some countries poses a particular risk to member states' tax revenues and to the equal and fair treatment of companies. in order to combat tax havens, it advocates, in particular, withholding tax in the case of payments from the member states to entities practising tax secrecy or opacity. the report also calls for better tax cooperation between member states, a necessary step in the process of european integration. i supported this text because it calls for tackling the root causes of tax evasion, by proposing reforms at the level of the union but also at the level of the member states. in addition, it is accompanied by a monitoring mechanism to ensure the proper implementation of the directive and the uniform interpretation of its measures by the member states.
in writing. ‒ my colleague and socialist comrade hugues bayet's report on tax evasion affirms the european parliament's ambition to restore justice and equality in taxation. the recent revelations (swissleaks, panama papers, luxleaks, etc.) have had the merit of putting the fight against tax evasion back at the top of the political agenda. the socialists and democrats have set out a principle: taxes must be paid where the profits are made. to achieve this, the report proposed important steps: capping interest deductions, establishing a strict blacklist of tax havens common to the 28 member states, and limiting the use of patent filings, too often used to artificially reduce profits. this is a good thing, and taxes should not be avoided, because they are the foundation of a just society. there is no reason why those who pay their taxes should suffer the evasion of others. this report is encouraging, and we must go further by introducing public country-by-country reporting of multinationals. this is the best way to track profits efficiently.
in writing. ‒ in january 2016, the commission presented a set of measures in a directive to combat tax evasion by groups of companies. this directive is central because it tackles the most common and costly mechanisms for public finances, at the heart of avoidance schemes. six points: capping the deductibility of interest, taxing the outflow of latent capital gains, the introduction of switchover clauses, a general anti-abuse clause, rules for the shifting of profits from parent companies to foreign companies under control and less taxed, and the case of hybrid schemes generating non-taxation. the bayet report has made some changes to the commission's draft. the european parliament is not a co-legislator here, and as with all taxation matters, the council will retain the final say. at its meeting at the end of may, the ministers of the 28 member states failed to reach agreement, partly because of the opposition of the netherlands and ireland. it seems appropriate to continue along this line and to support these advances which will be in the interest of national public finances. i vote for it.
in writing. ‒ in the wake of the luxleaks, the european commission is reportedly keen to make proposals to put a stop to these practices. the proposal for a directive submitted to the european parliament aims to 'set rules to combat tax evasion'. the aim is to ensure that companies pay their taxes where they make their profits and thus to define precisely the conditions for the establishment of multinational companies. the commission also proposes to set up a european tax identification number to facilitate the automatic exchange of tax data, which many companies refuse to disclose. the report proposes to establish a new blacklist of tax havens at european level and to include good governance clauses in tax matters in trade agreements and economic partnership agreements with third countries. in view of the panama papers scandal, this would indeed be a necessary minimum. unfortunately, while parliament has obtained improvements on the commission's original text, it is still a missed opportunity. definitions and obligations remain too vague, especially with regard to multinationals. i am not saying that we should not be doing more to restore the confidence of european citizens, so i abstained.

in writing. ‒ there is no doubt that space development needs to be addressed in a comprehensive approach at the level of the european union. it is impossible for a single european state to have sufficient resources to develop the many existing and future space technologies. this is particularly true in the current climate of insecurity, the rise of terrorism and the influx of migrants. the union must allow, in the context of intergovernmental cooperation, the use of its space capabilities to monitor, for example, terrorist training camps by means of its satellites, or to anticipate migratory floods on our coasts and stop them before these boats of fortune run aground. we all have an interest in the development of joint civil programmes such as galileo, copernicus and airbus, which are the real successes of european technological and commercial cooperation. the european space agency must be able to play an important role in the definition and implementation of a european space policy and it must fully integrate the security and defence policy of the european union.

for the greens/efa group madam president, improving the exchange of data is an essential element in order to better combat terrorism. the transnational dimension of the most serious crimes requires greater cooperation in this area and more effective use of european databases, while ensuring respect for fundamental rights, in particular in the area of data protection. in this respect, the principle of purpose limitation is very important: a database which is used for a specific purpose should not suddenly be used for other purposes. for example, the schengen information system contains data on innocent persons, such as missing persons, which should not be interconnected with databases related to terrorism, as there is no link between the two. if we are to move towards greater interoperability of european databases, it is essential to also provide for a harmonised data protection framework. the two are and must be linked. this is necessary to avoid fragmentation, because the new directive on data protection in the police field does not cover the databases in question here, such as the schengen information system. the establishment of a common set of data protection rules must therefore be an integral part of this path towards greater interoperability. it is a question of the coherence and efficiency of our system, and above all of the protection of our fundamental rights.

of sources are the conditions for an informed judgment. the cross-referencing of sources is absolutely necessary for parliamentary work. in this connection, i had already supported the plan of our intelligence officials to set up a school of economic warfare in 1986, because war today is often economic and involves the manipulation of information, and this when i was in the office of the president of the national assembly. i also think that parliamentary investigative work is fundamental, because there is a constant attempt to manipulate us, to manipulate the representatives of sovereignty. i must say, however, that the experience of two years in this parliament makes me doubt our sincerity in seeking the truth. i am not talking about the commission, it is under pressure, as our investigative journalists have shown in their book, circus politicus, which has received the international press prize. this commission manipulates us with false information, which is the product of state propaganda, of commissioners linked to circles of hidden interests that have nothing european about them. this propaganda is shameless, outrageous, carried out by disinformation agencies presented as emanations of civil society or by these secret societies working for foreign lobbies. there is enough precision in the investigative work done by journalists. i am talking about our parliament, about the way we take information, and about the way we look at the information we receive. we are quantitatively more than well informed, but qualitatively, are we really well informed? i'm asking you. our foreign services, for example, do not work with sources, do not oversee the intelligence work done by our states. on the other hand, in france, for example, there is a real work which is also being done in the national parliament. there's no such job here. parliament is the place where the propaganda, the lying, so-called official voice, is amplified. we write reports, we hold meetings, often in all directions, but in the same tone and with the same people, in the same ideological approach. it's not a scientific approach. our so-called independent experts are chosen from the same mainstream of single-mindedness formatted in the world of fiction versus reality. in doing so, we distill, under the guise of analysis, propaganda and ideology, which, when transformed into decisions, explain the harmfulness of parliament's action, which continues on the path of lies. the commission has always supported the policy of chaos promoted by the united states, without acknowledging its mistakes, which the american executive is now acknowledging. during the iraq war, the commission, and particularly its leader, was the faithful relay, the worst amplifier of the
