in writing. ‒ last april, as socialists, we welcomed the presentation by the european commission of an action plan on vat, a necessary first step. the report adopted today in plenary allows us to go further. it should be recalled that crossborder vat fraud represents an annual loss of €50 billion for france. in total, more than €170 billion is lost every year, when governments need this money to invest, innovate and create jobs. the future vat system must be based on the destination principle: it must be paid where goods and services are consumed. i am pleased that all the s&d requests have been taken into account in this report: the unanimity required to revise the vat system is the major difficulty, which is why i think it is important that the council listens to the european parliament. finally, in parallel with this reform, i welcome the announcement by mr moscovici of a specific proposal to align vat rates on digital books and online presses with those on paper media.
in writing. ‒ the commission announced in april a number of initiatives to combat vat fraud. the current system dates from 1993 and was intended to be transitional, but is not adapted to the digital age, creates numerous additional costs, especially for smes and cross-border transactions, and encourages fraud. to remedy this, the commission proposes the abandonment of the principle of taxation in the country of origin, short-term measures against fraud, more freedom for states to set rates and specific measures for electronic commerce. the report mainly endorses the abandonment of the principle of taxation in the country of origin in favour of that of the country of destination. this is the measure most contested by the professionals. in practice, the supplier of goods or services will collect vat from his customer and, if he resides abroad, by applying the foreign rate. the main risk is that the system will quickly become unmanageable, as firms selling to exporters will have to juggle the 89 rates in force in the union. the commission could use this as an argument to impose its ultimate solution, namely the harmonization of rates, more effectively in the future. i abstained.
in writing. ‒ the vat issue is important to consider, as it generated almost €1 trillion in 2014, or around 7% of european gdp. to date, nothing has been done to prevent the fraud, which amounts to a considerable amount. the reduction of distortions of competition is therefore necessary to try to stop these fraudulent practices. the consolidation of the system is a priority and must be accompanied by new mechanisms. for these reasons, i voted in favour of this text.
in writing. ‒ this report starts from an obvious observation, the need to fight fraud, to arrive at a complex and unfinished project. it confirms the abandonment of the principle of taxation in the country of origin for that of the country of destination. in practice, the supplier of goods or services will collect vat from his customer and, if he resides abroad, by applying the foreign rate. the situation could quickly become unmanageable and give the commission ammunition to carry out its project, which is the harmonization of rates. however, there are significant positive aspects, including a reduction in the administrative burden for smes. i therefore abstained on that vote.
in writing. ‒ i abstained on this report, which has some positive elements, unfortunately counterbalanced by other more negative points. the current vat system, which dates back to 1993, is no longer adapted to the realities of today's world, especially in the face of the challenges posed by the digital age and the administrative and financial burdens borne by smes. according to the commission, this mismatch would represent €170 billion in annual shortfalls and almost €50 billion in fraud. however, the solutions proposed by the commission and, even worse, the econ report on this subject, completely miss the mark of an updating of the system for the benefit of enterprises. the principle of taxation in the country of origin being abandoned in favour of the country of destination is rejected by the professionals. we know that behind this lies a real strategy of shock, with the commission seeking to create a cacophony in order to better impose, in the long run, its system of 'harmonisation of rates' and thus create a 'european vat', which would deprive the member states of a significant part of their tax revenues (50% for the french budget).
in writing. ‒ this report aims to combat vat fraud, estimated at €50 billion. to remedy this, the european commission presented a proposal last april that includes the abandonment of the principle of taxation in the country of origin, more freedom for member states to set rates and specific measures for e-commerce. however, the report is wary of the effectiveness of these proposals, considering that they rely on the ability of national governments to coordinate better. it is therefore called for the generalization of self-liquidation for transactions between professionals. this will place the burden of payment on the last link in the chain, making the system even more vulnerable to fraud. moreover, with the abandonment of the principle of taxation in the country of origin, our exporters will have to constantly juggle with the 89 vat rates in force in the union, thus giving the european commission an additional argument to impose on the states a harmonisation of rates. i have, however, abstained on this report, which seeks to provide concrete answers to combat tax evasion.
in writing. ‒ the union has no power in taxation except for indirect taxation: vat and excise duties (alcohol, tobacco, oil). part of vat revenue is an own resource of the union, representing €17.667 billion of the european budget, or 12.27% of the total revenue of the union. we need a european vat framework to prevent member states from changing the vat rate to bring down the cost of goods or services and thus create unfair competition. that is why we have the vat directive, which sets a minimum standard rate of 15%. however, we must go further and create a genuine, definitive vat system which will offer more convergence while leaving flexibility for member states to set their rates. the commission will also be able to use the european system to combat vat fraud more effectively. i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report is based on the european commission's communication of 7 april 2016 on the vat action plan. in its action plan, the commission announced that it would present a legislative proposal for a definitive vat system. the current eu vat system has been in force since 1993, but was designed as a transitional arrangement, not to become definitive. i had concentrated on the question of reduced rates and the list of activities which could benefit from these reduced rates. the existence of such schemes can sometimes help to maintain economic and structural activity in rural areas, such as those of equestrian centres. i hope that, even though there is a need to simplify the european vat system and to fight against fraud, this reduced rate system will remain flexible and effective. for these reasons i voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ since 1993, taxation of trade in goods and services between member states has been governed by an arrangement, then envisaged as transitional . this system, which is now difficult to describe as 'provisional' since it has been in force for 23 years, is proving to be very complex as vat rates differ from one state to another, with significantly unequal levels for the same products. the commission announced in april 2016 that it intended to establish a definitive vat scheme, aimed at harmonising existing arrangements and rates. the level will then be set freely by the national authorities, provided that it respects a minimum rate to avoid unfair competition. i therefore supported this report, which proposes a simplification of the existing rules and provides for the principle of taxation in the country where the property is used. this will, on the one hand, make it easier for companies involved in international trade to read the data and, on the other hand, remove the uncertainties created by the system, which make it more vulnerable to fraud.

in writing. ‒ the vat system, which was introduced in 1993, was a first step, a transitional system. fragmented, complex and costly, it needs to be reformed to enable the european single market to offer businesses a simple vat environment. the commission will launch a reform in 2017 on the subject (vat/smes, e-commerce, administrative cooperation and eurofisc). the aim is to achieve a harmonised european vat system that facilitates trade and ensures fair competition. the langen report prepares parliament's position on this future reform. the self-liquidation mechanism was the focus of the negotiations. some countries (czech republic, austria) are very much in favour of the general use of this system, as they believe it would reduce vat fraud - which is higher in these countries. as socialists and as french people, we are formally opposed to this, since it would only shift the problem to the neighbouring member states. it is a non-cooperative solution for europe. finally, all the red lines and requests of the social democrats were taken into account, in particular the financial services which must be subject to vat and the requirement of convergence of vat rates. i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ since 1993, the vat system in force in the european union has been designed as a transitional system. the 'taxation of trade between member states' must be replaced by a definitive system based on the principle of taxation of supplies of goods and services in the member state of origin. the council shall adopt appropriate directives with a view to completing the common system of vat and, in particular, to progressively restricting or abolishing derogations from that system. with the aim of 'creating a single vat area in the union, which is a pillar for a thorough internal market'. this report follows that logic. it is designed to reinforce this unfair tax system. it also proposes to 'limit the exceptions' to the normal rate of vat, which would be tantamount to restricting the exemption for basic necessities. i am voting against this profoundly unfair text.

on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, finally, we have this debate in the european parliament's plenary on the most important foreign policy issue for our continent, namely africa and its access to energy, because the figures speak for themselves: out of more than 1 billion africans, 700 million have no access to electricity. by 2030, if nothing is done, this number could rise to 1.3 billion. in other words, it is the future most populous continent on the planet that will have the least access to electricity and light. can we accept this in a decent way for a continent that is only ten kilometres away from us and with which we share so much, both historically and culturally? i don't think so, we don't think so, but it is a fact. to this, of course, must be added the demographic prospect of a continent that will have nearly 2 billion inhabitants by 2050 and will suffer from climate change in its full force, with all that this implies in terms of food security, access to energy or tensions around the use of agricultural land. that is why, with about 40 colleagues, first through the committee on regional development chaired by linda mcavan, we wanted to have this debate in plenary this afternoon in the european parliament. i thank them for supporting me in this endeavor. our message is simple: let's go, it's time to help developing countries, and especially africa, to expand their access to energy. the stakes are enormous: education, economic development, but also migration, stability, security in a continent plagued by terrorism. this is what's behind the access to energy. ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, a lot is happening now because the african continent has understood the enormous opportunities that lie ahead. morocco has developed the world's largest solar thermal power plant in ouarzazate, which will provide clean energy to more than 1 million moroccans by 2018. another example is kenya, where only a third of the population has access to electricity, and which has developed the lake turkana wind farm. it is expected to generate 20 percent of kenya's energy by summer 2017. more generally, the hydraulic basins of central africa, the rift valley fault and the sunshine enjoyed by the continent in general are sources of hydropower, geothermal or solar energy that are unmatched in the rest of the world. at present, however, only a tiny fraction of this potential is exploited (only 7% of hydropower capacity and less than 1% of geothermal capacity) and photovoltaic initiatives are still too embryonic. we can feel the first signs of a continent which could become a renewable energy pool if it is properly supported, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen. for this, the continent needs our unconditional support and yours. yet, despite the urgency and consensus on the subject, one gets the feeling that the machine is having a hard time getting started. of the €10 billion pledged last year at cop21 - which i was the rapporteur for the european parliament - to the african renewable energy agency, only half has been provided by the most developed countries. however, there is no shortage of goodwill in the european commission, the european parliament, the member states and civil society. i am thinking in particular of the enormous work done by jean-louis borloo with his energy for africa initiative. now is the time to change course and implement this great marshall plan for energy access in africa, as called for by jean-louis borloo and his foundation. in this, i fully join his fight. that is the reason for our parliamentary action today: to help turn undeniable political will into concrete action. the cop22, which just ended last week in marrakech, carried a similar message. africa is the crucial issue for the next decades. so after the decisions, the action! with this great marshall plan for energy access, we have the opportunity to implement this great and beautiful action for the development of our neighbour. in this context, i welcome the launch by the european commission of the external investment facility. it seems to me absolutely necessary that such an instrument should be dedicated to energy access and be ready as soon as possible, in particular before the next eu-africa summit in autumn 2017, as proposed by the european commission. the marshall plan for the electrification of africa, the instruments for external investment, support for the african renewable energy agency: that is how, commissioner, we can, in a very concrete way, help the development of energy access on a continent which so badly needs it. i am waiting for you to give us the perspectives and the answers so that we can be in concrete action, commissioner. this is how we will put europe back at the centre of the international stage, given the many ramifications that depend on african development. in short, commissioner, let us go ahead and waste no more time!
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me first tell you about my experience. when i was head of the energy sector in alsace - it was my first job as a civil servant - i wanted to do something for africa. i didn't have the support of the regional council at the time, and i had obtained a million francs. with this money, in sanaga-maritime, in cameroon, we did rural electrification and, from this rural electrification, we started farms, a small carpentry shop and we also put around the infrastructure that goes with development, that is, water and health. electricity is therefore an indispensable means of development. it is a necessary condition, but it is not a sufficient condition. i will come back to that. i would like to begin by emphasizing the full support of our group for this initiative. 3.5 billion at union level is good. a billion for france is also good. all of this for targets that remain modest for 2020 because i'm not going to talk about 2030 with 300 gigawatts. let's do it with these 10 gigawatts first, which is quite possible. one gigawatt is about a billion. let me give you a methodology. for 20 years i have been working on africa's development in a private capacity, apart from my other professional activities in the regional institute for cooperation in the alsace region and the european institute for cooperation. first, we need to build on local african initiatives. i think that the initiative of youba sokona with the african development bank, the afd, kfw (kreditanstalt für wiederaufbau), is really what needs to be done, namely that we have development agencies at home and we have potential in africa. we have to work together. we must not create new structures. i like mr borloo very much, but i disagree with my colleague on this. secondly, we must have a multilateral approach and not just a european one. we have to be aware that it is very good to bring together the united arab emirates, the united states, china and russia. all available funding should be used with the coherence of african initiatives at local level. thirdly, and this is where i am addressing myself to you, commissioner, it is very important what i am about to say and i do not know whether you will hear it: we must avoid levers! leverage, it won't work! you have to invest where the people are and not necessarily where the money is and the profitability is, if you want to do rural development and if you really want to develop africa. where it's profitable, it'll do it all by itself anyway. so we need to have a marshall plan approach. the plan started with loans and ended with more than 90% donations. we need to have an approach where we are literally investing new money in this rural electrification and rural development. i would like to say that even colonial france was able to invest without the prospect of return on investment when it developed, for example, the entire sewerage system in douala or when it created the railway that connected the south to the north of cameroon. we were able to take a long-term view. fourthly, electricity is a necessary but not sufficient condition. electricity is a means, like a road. just because you have electricity or you have a road, it doesn't create wealth. it is a necessary but not sufficient condition. we must really build development programmes around electricity. i would like to see these programmes given priority in the countries most in need. i am thinking of course of the sub-saharan great lakes region, where there is still some stability, in cameroon, in the central african republic and then in the democratic republic of congo, with all its potential. i am also thinking of the maghreb, egypt and algeria. but i come back to what we need, which is a genuine marshall plan of donations by monetary creation, like france financed its power stations after the war. it did so by creating money. it was the treasury's advances to électricité de france that made this possible. it was money creation, pure money creation. we must do all this from a development perspective around industry if we are to be able to really put rural and local development first.
member of the commission. – mr president, the european commission is committed to the goal of assisting developing countries in providing energy access for 500 million people by 2030. this is of course a target that cannot be achieved by the eu funds alone; the contribution of all global actors will be required. today we estimate that the projects supported with eu funds under the current multiannual financial framework by 2020 will contribute to provide on-grid and off-grid access to energy for up to 40 million people, generate 6.5 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity and save 15 million tonnes of co2 per year in our developing country partners. i would like to thank the parliament for its full support and i am pleased to see that our visions of this subject are aligned.
president of the committee on budgets. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, at a time of instability in europe and the world, it is comforting that the european institutions can put aside their differences and give the union a budget within the time limits set by the treaties. contrary to the legend that every second year the conciliation failed, i am glad that in 2016, for the 2017 budget, as in 2015, for the 2016 budget, we reached an agreement. i am glad that this year, after many hours of negotiations, parliament and the council have taken a step towards each other to send two clear messages. the first message is that the priority remains, more than ever, to tackle the problem of migration by strengthening control of our external borders, while allowing the dignified reception of new arrivals and the humanely sustainable return of migrants who cannot claim refugee status. we should not be under any illusions, there is still a lot to be done in this area and our budget is extremely constrained in this area, but the progress of the budgetary authority for 2017 is undoubtedly in the right direction. the second message is that europe is investing in its youth: an additional €500 million will be made available for the youth employment initiative. in fact, one billion, if we add the additional appropriations from the european social fund. in addition, an additional 200 million was earmarked for future programmes such as support for smes, the interconnection of infrastructure in europe, erasmus+ for students and apprentices - vice-president of the commission. – mr president, this has been a very engaged session and i am very grateful for the comments that have been made. let me respond to some of the points that honourable members have raised. first, there are indeed grounds for concern about the level of payments in the budget for 2017 and, more specifically, about the level of payments for cohesion policy. it is unfortunate but true that the new programmes – the programmes under the current multiannual financial framework – have taken some time to start, with the result that in many of them we are registering delays in implementation. we have been working very hard with member states to encourage the availability of authorising bodies that can then certify expenditures so we can speed up implementation. that would, of course, have a positive impact on payments. so it is definitely not because we do not have the capacity to provide these funds. it is objectively because of the slower pace of the implementation of the programmes. we are working with the council – as minister lesay would confirm – to find ways to speed up that process. secondly, a number of speakers made comments about the new the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, we are in the midst of a debate which is absolutely crucial. it may seem technical since we are going to talk about the possible modification of a code of conduct and conflicts of interest. in reality, as you know, this debate is taking place in a very specific context for europe, at a time when european citizens are doubting, sometimes with good reason, that europe is defending the general interest, the common good, and not necessarily private interests or particular interests. so we have to be very careful about this. the question of transparency, control and the functioning of our institutions is, in the present state of the european question, of major importance. transparency is one of the pillars of democracy and more than ever we need to be exemplary in this respect. the situation has worsened recently. a number of debates, to use no strong words, have taken place, notably with the move of former commission president barroso to a private bank, goldman sachs, which had a very direct link with the financial crisis of 2008. of course, these factors must be taken into account. i sometimes wonder whether the commission is fully aware of this reality. when we asked commissioner moscovici, who was in your place recently, about this, he explained that there was no problem and that the code of conduct of the commission and the commissioners was perhaps among the best - i do not know if he did not even say "the best in the world"! to me, it's just a denial of reality; it's the coué method of saying that everything is fine. no, it's not all right! in order to change things, so that we can move towards more transparency and more control, two committees of this european parliament have unanimously approved, and i emphasize this, the two reports - the committee on budgetary control and the committee on legal affairs. this unanimity must also challenge the commission, since it shows how united the european parliament is in this effort to change rules which are currently not working. so, what's wrong? i will deal very briefly with two aspects, namely conflicts of interest and the code of conduct. let us first discuss conflicts of interest. at the moment when commissioners take office, at that stage, they are only required to declare what they themselves consider to be likely to create a conflict of interest. however, this concept is nowhere defined. so the first thing to do is to define what a conflict of interest is. we do so in this report, and we ask that the european parliament's legal affairs committee be able to check the financial statements and the assets in order to determine whether or not there is a conflict of interest. this is simply the application of the separation of powers. this is a major advance, and it must be implemented. we ask the same thing during the term of office, when there is a change in assets, financial interests or portfolio. that is the question of conflicts of interest and naturally this requirement must be extended to family interests as is the case during the mandate. the second question is the question of the code of ethics and the code of good conduct. at this stage, you, commissioner, and all your colleagues, have a duty of honesty and delicacy. it's not defined anywhere. define honesty and delicacy. ensure that the ethics committee, which is currently in charge of monitoring, is composed of independent experts and is completely free from pressure from private interests or the commission. i would add a third element. we ask you to ensure that during the three years following your term of office you do not have the opportunity to go to work in the private sector in sectors which you have had to deal with in your capacity as commissioner. commissioners are paid for this; it's not outrageous. you see, the changes we're asking for are not excessive. what is needed is simply an alignment of the commission's rules of operation with what is happening in all democracies around the world.

in writing. ‒ the parliamentary committee recommended that parliament adopt its position at first reading by adopting the commission's proposal. the european regulation establishing the union customs code excludes the application of certain provisions to goods which have temporarily left the customs territory of the union by moving between two union ports or airports without a stopover outside the union. the excluded provisions subject to the amendment concern the following obligations: to lodge an entry summary declaration; to notify the arrival of a seagoing vessel or aircraft; transport the goods to specified places and present them to the customs authorities at the place where they are unloaded or transhipped; the temporary deposit. there is currently no legal basis for requiring the presentation of goods that are unloaded or transhipped at the point where the goods are re-introduced into the customs territory of the union after temporarily leaving it, which makes it more difficult for the customs authorities to monitor the goods. i voted in favour of this report, which therefore aims to fill a legal vacuum and to contribute to more efficient customs supervision.

in writing. ‒ i supported this report on the european commission's amendment of article 136 of the customs code of the european union. this amendment will improve the customs supervision of goods when they enter the union through a port or airport and are then transported to a second port in the union where they are unloaded. the aim is to clarify the legal status of these goods and to ensure proper customs supervision of goods moving within the european union.
in writing. ‒ the original regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing the union customs code excludes the application of certain provisions to goods which have temporarily left the customs territory of the union by moving between two union ports or airports without a stopover outside the union. the excluded provisions subject to the amendment concern the following obligations: to lodge an entry summary declaration; to notify the arrival of a seagoing vessel or aircraft; transport the goods to specified places and present them to the customs authorities at the place where they are unloaded or transhipped; the temporary deposit. as a result, there is no legal basis today to require the presentation of goods that are unloaded or transhipped at the place where the goods are re-introduced into the customs territory of the union after temporarily leaving it. this makes it more difficult for the customs authorities to monitor the goods. the proposal to amend the regulation is therefore intended to fill this legal vacuum and to contribute to a somewhat more efficient customs supervision. i voted yes.
in writing. ‒ this report concerns a proposal for a regulation postponing by one year the date of application of regulation 1286/2014 on key information documents for insurance-based retail investment products (priips). regulation (eu) no 1286/2014 introduced a series of measures to strengthen investor protection in the financial services sector by improving the transparency of the retail investment market. it requires the originator of retail packaged and insurance-based investment products to produce a key information document, called a key information document (kid). that regulation empowers the esas to develop regulatory technical standards specifying the elements to be contained in the kid. on 30 june 2016, the commission approved the draft submitted by the esas by means of a delegated act which was also approved by the council. however, on 14 september 2016, the european parliament rejected the delegated act and requested the commission to review the provisions on multiple option priips, performance scenarios and notices indicating that a product may be difficult to understand. in order to avoid legal instability, i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ this regulation empowers the european supervisory authorities (esas) to develop regulatory technical standards specifying the elements that key information documents (kids) should contain. on 30 june 2016, the commission approved the draft submitted by the esas by means of a delegated act which was also approved by the council. i was opposed to that delegated act at the time; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the information contained in the dic is not used for other purposes. that is why i have approved this proposal for a regulation.
in writing. ‒ regulation 1286/2014 introduced a series of measures to strengthen investor protection in the financial services sector, allowing for an improvement in the transparency of the retail investment market. it requires the originator of a retail packaged insurance-based investment product (priip) to produce a key information document, called a key information document (kid). the kids that inform investors are not clear enough, and moreover, often too optimistic. the proposal for a regulation to decide on technical standards specifying the information to be contained in kids. i will not oppose it, preferring legal stability for investors.
in writing. ‒ i am rather in favour of postponing the date of application of this regulation, which currently has many shortcomings, for example: kids no longer present past data but only future assumptions; these kids are relatively opaque as regards the performance of products and the way they are calculated; the risk to the investor is not sufficiently highlighted. i therefore vote in favour of this proposal for a regulation and this report, which call for the date of application to be postponed.
in writing. ‒ regulation no 1286/2014 aims to strengthen investor protection in financial markets by improving the transparency of insurance-based retail packaged investment products (priips), in particular through the creation of a key information document, called a key information document (kid). although the idea is sound, the kid is criticized for being opaque and for not sufficiently warning investors of the risks of losses that may exceed the amount of capital invested. priip promoters are not required to present past performance in their kids, which leaves a lot of room for subjectivity in presenting future performance. the text calls for a delay of 12 months from the date of application of the regulation, which is scheduled for 1 january 2017, in order to allow sufficient time to re-enter certain information in the kid. although we are not against the regulation, we believe that its entry into force without the technical standards specifying the information to be contained in the kid would lead to legal instability. that is why i voted in favour of this text.
in writing. ‒ this report follows a proposal by the european commission to improve investor protection measures for the main investment products purchased by small investors. in this context, the european parliament considers that small investors should be better informed about the possible costs of investment products. i fully share the principle of preventing and defending the interests of small investors by introducing simple and clear rules and guidelines, which is why i voted in favour of this text.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report which seeks to postpone the date of application of the regulation on key information documents for insurance-based retail investment products. while i am in favour of the production of key information documents on financial products, i nevertheless consider that the proper application of a regulation requires that the relevant actors be given sufficient time for preparation. the detailed content of these information documents has only been established since 30 june 2016. the commission has also provided information on the implementation of the new rules on the protection of personal data. it is therefore necessary to defer the date of application of this regulation to 1 january 2018.

in writing. this report asks the european parliament to approve an agreement providing for visa-free travel for citizens of the union and nationals of kiribati who are travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. the report is accompanied by a justification stating that the agreement is an outcome between the eu and third countries - which has a strong political significance in the context of the cotonou agreement - and an additional means of strengthening economic and cultural relations and intensifying political dialogue on various issues (human rights, fundamental freedoms, etc.). the libe committee, however, invites the european commission to monitor possible developments with regard to issues relating to illegal immigration, public order and security, the union's external relations with the third country concerned, including, in particular, considerations related to respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms . the visa waiver therefore presents security risks (organised crime, money laundering, drug trafficking, etc.) and immigration risks. that is why i opposed this report.
in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the union and nationals of kiribati who are travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. such a visa exemption would present security risks (organised crime, money laundering, drug trafficking, etc.) and immigration risks. is it appropriate to conclude visa waiver agreements at a time when the risk of terrorist attacks is real and the european union has lost all control of mass immigration? i voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the union and nationals of kiribati who are travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. at a time when europe is being hit by terrorist attacks and massive illegal immigration, these exemptions do not seem to be on the agenda, as bad people could one day use them. i am therefore strongly opposed to it.
in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the union and nationals of kiribati who are travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. the rapporteur believes that this type of agreement is a means of strengthening economic and cultural relations and of intensifying dialogue on various issues, notably human rights and fundamental freedoms. on the contrary, we consider it absolutely inappropriate to conclude such an agreement at a time when our western societies are threatened by islamic fundamentalism which uses legal immigration routes to enter our territories and plan terrorist attacks there. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. that is why i voted against this text.
in writing. i voted in favour of the conclusion of the agreement between the european union and kiribati on the short-stay visa waiver. this visa-free regime for citizens of the union and nationals of kiribati for a maximum stay of 90 days in any 180-day period should strengthen our economic and cultural relations by having a positive impact on both contracting parties.
in writing. - i voted against this text. these agreements provide for visa-free travel for citizens of the union and of kiribati, the solomon islands, micronesia, tuvalu and the marshall islands who are travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. in a context of security concerns, any proposal for visa facilitation or exemptions seems to us inappropriate.
in writing. ‒ since the beginning of its mandate, this parliament has been required to approve 18 agreements with third countries aimed at exempting eu and third country nationals from visa requirements when travelling to the territory of the other party for non-business stays of less than 3 months. i voted against all of them, including the five agreements today. the latter are, of course, small island states in oceania with a total population of barely one million. the theoretical risks they pose in terms of mass immigration, terrorism or organised crime seem marginal. but on the one hand, this is part of a general desire in brussels to liberalize visa policy as much as possible with as many countries as possible, including the most unstable and most criminogenic countries. on the other hand, among the 18 states concerned, there are many countries on various national, european or international lists of tax havens or countries which do not cooperate in the fight against tax evasion or money laundering. this policy contributes to the insecurity and vulnerability of our countries. it must stop immediately.
in writing. ‒ if we take the specific case of the kiribati islands, i see no particular difficulty in lifting the short-stay visa requirement, i.e. three months over a period of 180 days, for nationals of these three archipelagos of 100,000 inhabitants located in the pacific ocean. there are no migration or security risks. however, i believe that visa exemption should not be an automatic process but the result of a thorough assessment of the political, institutional and geostrategic situation of the country concerned and of the possible repercussions that a lifting of the visa requirement may have on the european territory. this review should not only be based on the progress made in the years preceding this evaluation but also take into account the potential risks of air pollution that a visa exemption may create in the medium term as we have seen with some countries in the western balkans. i therefore reiterate my support for the swift adoption of the suspension mechanism which recalls that the visa waiver is not an 'unlimited pass' but a conditional facility which meets certain requirements.
in writing. ‒ this report on a visa waiver for kiribati citizens raises pro-forma security risks. as such, it would be very unwise for the european union to sign an agreement that would only add to the already heavy weight of the migration crisis in our territories. i therefore voted against.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which provides for the conclusion of an agreement with the republic of kiribati to facilitate the issuing of short-stay visas.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report because it is not appropriate to conclude visa-free agreements at a time when the european union has lost all control over immigration.

in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the union and the third-country nationals concerned who are travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. the libe committee, however, invites the european commission to 'observe possible developments with regard to issues relating to illegal immigration, public order and security, the union's external relations with the third country concerned, including, in particular, considerations relating to respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms'. the visa waiver therefore presents security risks (organised crime, money laundering, drug trafficking, etc.) and immigration risks. the question must be asked whether it is appropriate to conclude visa-free agreements at a time when the risk of terrorist attacks is real and when the european union has lost all control over mass immigration. i vote against.
in writing. ‒ the proposed visa waiver poses security risks (organised crime, money laundering, drug trafficking, etc.). it is not appropriate to vote for such an agreement when we see every day that the eu is unable to control migration flows. i am voting against this text.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which provides, on a reciprocal basis and for short stays, for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the european union and micronesian nationals. this agreement will strengthen the economic and cultural links between these countries and our continent.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on the visa waiver for the territories of the eu and the federated states of micronesia. this exemption applies to all travellers from both zones, for a period of 90 days, for any reason. however, it excludes persons wishing to work for a salary. this agreement opens a new stage in our rapprochement. this remains paramount as europe negotiates a comprehensive economic partnership agreement with the federated states of micronesia.
in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the union and its nationals travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. the report is accompanied by a brief justification stating that it constitutes a culmination of the deepening of bilateral relations which has a strong political significance in the context of the cotonou agreement. the libe committee, however, invites the european commission to 'observe possible developments with regard to issues relating to illegal immigration, public order and security, the union's external relations with this country, including, in particular, considerations relating to respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms'. the visa waiver therefore presents security risks (organised crime, money laundering, drug trafficking, etc.) and immigration risks. the question must be asked whether it is appropriate to conclude visa-free agreements at a time when the risk of terrorist attacks is real and when the european union has lost all control over mass immigration. i vote against it.
in writing. this report asks for the european parliament's approval of an agreement providing for visa-free travel for citizens of the union and tuvalu nationals travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. the report is accompanied by a justification stating that the agreement is an outcome between the eu and tuvalu - with strong political significance in the context of the cotonou agreement - and an additional means of strengthening economic and cultural relations and intensifying political dialogue on various issues (human rights, fundamental freedoms, etc.). the libe committee, however, invites the european commission to 'observe possible developments with regard to issues relating to illegal immigration, public order and security, the union's external relations with the third country concerned, including, in particular, considerations relating to respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms'. the visa waiver therefore presents security risks (organised crime, money laundering, drug trafficking, etc.) and immigration risks. that is why i opposed this report.

in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the union and tuvalu who are travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. at a time when europe is being hit by terrorist attacks and massive illegal immigration, these exemptions do not seem to be on the agenda, as bad people could one day use them. i am therefore strongly opposed to it.
in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for a visa-free travel regime for citizens of the union and tuvalu who are travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. the rapporteur believes that this type of agreement is a means of strengthening economic and cultural relations and of intensifying dialogue on various issues, notably human rights and fundamental freedoms. on the contrary, we consider it absolutely inappropriate to conclude such an agreement at a time when our western societies are threatened by islamic fundamentalism which uses legal immigration routes to enter our territories and plan terrorist attacks there. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. that is why i voted against this text.

in writing. ‒ if we take the particular case of tuvalu, i see no particular difficulty in lifting the short-stay visa requirement, i.e. three months over a period of 180 days, for nationals of this polynesian archipelago of 12 000 inhabitants in the pacific ocean. there are no migration or security risks. however, i believe that visa exemption should not be an automatic process but the result of a thorough assessment of the political, institutional and geostrategic situation of the country concerned and of the possible repercussions that a lifting of the visa requirement may have on the european territory. this review should not only be based on the progress made in the years preceding this evaluation but also take into account the potential risks of air pollution that a visa exemption may create in the medium term as we have seen with some countries in the western balkans. i therefore reiterate my support for the swift adoption of the suspension mechanism which recalls that the visa waiver is not an 'unlimited pass' but a conditional facility which meets certain requirements.
in writing. ‒ this report on a visa exemption for tuvalu citizens raises protective security risks. as such, it would be very unwise for the european union to sign an agreement that would only add to the already heavy weight of the migration crisis in our territories. i therefore voted against.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which provides for the conclusion of an agreement with tuvalu to facilitate the issuing of short-stay visas.

in writing. created in 2002 following severe floods, the european union solidarity fund (eusf) aims to provide financial assistance to member states and candidate countries that have suffered extraordinary natural disasters, with direct material damage amounting to more than eur 3 billion or representing more than 0.6% of gross national income. this report simplifies the procedures for mobilising the eusf in order to facilitate the execution of payments. to achieve this, the report recommends raising the threshold for advance payments from 10% to 15% and lowering the threshold for natural disasters to 1% of regional gdp. in addition, it is requested that other indicators, apart from gdp, such as the human development index and the regional development index, be taken into account in the new methods for calculating the allocation of the eusf. the eusf is the expression of european solidarity and provides significant financial support to national and local authorities in regions affected by natural disasters. in this context, it is appropriate to simplify the functioning of the eusf and to facilitate the execution of payments. i therefore voted in favour of this text.
in writing. ‒ this report aims to simplify the procedures for mobilising the european union solidarity fund (eusf) to facilitate the execution of payments to states affected by natural disasters. to achieve this, the text recommends, in particular, raising the threshold for advance payments from 10% to 15% and lowering the threshold for the eligibility of natural disasters to 1% of regional gdp. in addition, it is requested that other indicators, apart from gdp, such as the human development index and the regional development index, be taken into account in the new methods for calculating the allocation of the eusf. the fund provides significant financial support to regions affected by natural disasters. i therefore voted in favour of the proposal as it seems quite appropriate to simplify the operation of the eusf and to facilitate the execution of payments.
in writing. ‒ the eusf was established in 2002 and has a budget of €500 million to provide financial assistance to member states and candidate countries that have suffered extraordinary natural disasters with direct material damage of more than €3 billion or representing more than 0.6% of gross national income. the report should simplify the procedures for mobilising the eusf in order to facilitate the execution of payments to states affected by natural disasters, in particular by raising the threshold for advance payments or by taking into account other indicators in addition to gdp. in the face of natural disasters, financial support is always appropriate and welcome and the eusf is a significant tool for national or local authorities in the affected regions. so i decided to vote for it.
in writing. ‒ this report aims to facilitate the procedures for the implementation of the eusf in the event of natural disasters, both at regional and national level. i consider solidarity to be a virtue that can be exercised at european level, and i am therefore not against it. i therefore vote in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ this report aims to simplify the procedures for mobilising the european union solidarity fund (eusf) to facilitate the execution of payments to states affected by natural disasters. to achieve this, the report recommends raising the threshold for advance payments from 10% to 15% and lowering the threshold for natural disasters to 1% of regional gdp. in addition, it is requested that other indicators, apart from gdp, such as the human development index or the regional development index, be taken into account in the new methods for calculating the allocation of the eusf. we consider the eusf to be the expression of european solidarity and to be a significant financial support for national and local authorities in regions affected by natural disasters. in this context, it seems to us quite appropriate to simplify the operation of the eusf and to facilitate the execution of payments on the sole condition that it is not used to finance the reception of illegal migrants in the european union. i therefore voted in favour of this text.
in writing. ‒ the european union solidarity fund is an important source of financial support for local and regional authorities and helps to alleviate the consequences of natural disasters occurring across the european continent. these include floods, earthquakes, forest fires and other disasters that are often unpredictable and have major social, economic and environmental consequences. in the face of these threats, european solidarity is indispensable. unfortunately, it is noted that beneficiaries continue to face problems due to the length of the entire process of applying for advance payments. i voted in favour of this report which proposes improvements to the eusf for rapid and effective financial assistance to the victims of climate change and its most violent consequences.
in writing. ‒ the european union solidarity fund (eusf) was set up following the disastrous floods in central europe in the summer of 2002. it is an instrument for the eu to respond to major natural disasters on its territory. this european parliament report analyses the annual report of the eusf of the european commission and makes recommendations for a future reform that would redefine regional natural disasters. the report also calls on the european commission to analyse the possibility of increasing the threshold for advance payments to 15% and of reducing the processing times for applications to 4 weeks in order to increase the effectiveness of the eusf. considering that a more responsive and efficient fund would make it possible to respond better to the challenges of natural disasters that eu territories may face, i voted in favour of this report.

in writing. ‒ i voted for the gue and alde resolutions, as they call for referral to the court of justice to verify the compatibility of the eu-us agreement on the protection of personal data with the treaties. these texts underline that the european data protection supervisor raised questions on the compatibility of the framework agreement with the charter and european secondary data protection law, and in particular on the right to judicial redress, access to personal data by law enforcement agencies, limitation of the right of access to data of data subjects and data retention periods. the european data protection supervisor is also concerned that the competent data protection authorities in the united states do not meet the requirements of the court of justice to be considered fully independent and have effective powers of intervention, and is concerned about whether the data protection authorities will be able to block transfers of personal data if they do not comply with union law.
in writing. ‒ this is a motion for a resolution requesting the court of justice to give its opinion on the compatibility with the treaties of the proposed agreement between the united states of america and the european union on the protection of personal data processed for the purposes of the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of criminal offences. these texts underline that the european data protection supervisor raised a number of issues on the compatibility of the framework agreement with the charter and european secondary data protection law, and more specifically on the right to judicial redress, access to personal data by law enforcement agencies, limitation of the right of access to data of data subjects and data retention periods. these issues are relevant and legitimate, and i therefore supported this resolution and voted against the albrecht report on the agreement between the united states of america and the european union on the protection of personal data processed in the context of criminal offences.
in writing. ‒ on these resolutions concerning the opinion of the court of justice on the compatibility with the treaties of the agreement between the united states of america and the european union on the protection of personal data processed for the purposes of the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of criminal offences, i supported the alde resolution and voted against the gue resolution. the centrist resolution calls for the court of justice to be seized to verify the compatibility of the eu-us agreement on the protection of personal data with the treaties. the edps also fears that the competent data protection authorities in the united states do not meet the requirements of the court of justice to be considered fully independent and have effective powers of intervention, and is concerned about whether the data protection authorities will be able to block transfers of personal data if they do not comply with union data protection legislation.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the gue and alde resolutions, which call for the court of justice of the european union to be seized to verify the compatibility of the eu-us agreement on the protection of personal data with the treaties. the european data protection supervisor is concerned that the competent data protection authorities in the united states do not meet the requirements of the court of justice to be considered fully independent and to have effective powers of intervention, and is concerned about whether the data protection authorities will be able to block transfers of personal data if they do not comply with union data protection legislation. i voted against the albrecht report.
in writing. ‒ this motion for a resolution asks the court of justice to be consulted on the compatibility of the european treaties with the proposed agreement between the united states and the european union on the protection of personal data processed for the purposes of prevention, investigation and prosecution of criminal offences. the european data protection supervisor raised a number of questions about the inadequacy of data protection safeguards, in particular as regards the right to legal redress, the limitation of the right of access to data of data subjects and the period of data retention. the european data protection supervisor also doubts the full independence of the us data protection authorities, which is an essential prerequisite for such an agreement. that is why i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution.

in writing. ‒ i voted for these texts. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of personal data in the context of the protection of the rights of the individual. the european data protection supervisor expressed serious reservations, in particular regarding the independence of the us competent authorities and their ability to oppose an illegal transfer of personal data.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the two motions for resolutions tabled today, which seek the opinion of the luxembourg court of justice on the compatibility of an international agreement with the treaties. the purpose of the eu-us privacy shield is to protect the rights of eu citizens when their personal data is transferred to the us under other eu or bilateral agreements. the very definitions of 'personal data' and 'data processing' are known to differ on both sides of the atlantic, which is itself a problem. it is also known that rights of access, rectification and redress are limited in the united states for foreign nationals, despite the judicial redress act of february 2016. even the european data protection supervisor considers that this agreement does not provide sufficient guarantees as to the effectiveness of the remedies. the privacy act of 1974, for example, has not been amended. neither the eu nor its member states are considered to be entities whose citizens can bring civil actions against certain us agencies. all of this should be done with the utmost caution.

in writing. the agreement in question aims to establish a framework of principles and safeguards for the protection of personal data when transferred for criminal law enforcement purposes between the united states and the european union or its member states. its objective is to ensure a high level of protection of personal data of union data subjects when exchanged with the united states. with the front national, i oppose the very principle of systematic exchange of personal data. this agreement provides for certain rights and safeguards in relation to data protection, but these are insufficient. the european data protection supervisor recommends essential improvements to ensure that the judicial redress provisions are effective. it also states that mass transfers of sensitive data are not allowed. in addition, the european union or its member states have not yet been declared by the us department of justice as one of the countries whose citizens can bring civil actions against certain us government agencies under the privacy act of 1974. i therefore voted against.

for the greens/efa group madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we had a historic opportunity to improve rail transport and we missed it. this fourth railway package is the culmination of a long process begun 25 years ago by the european commission. we would have liked to have a real european railway, a railway that could compete with road and other polluting modes of transport, because, i would remind you, rail transport is the most environmentally friendly mode of transport, the one that emits the least co2 and fine particles. we have no choice but to increase the share of trains in europe, and if we want to achieve the greenhouse gas reduction targets, well we have not given ourselves enough means, even though we have the paris agreements. this aspect, which we shall vote on on wednesday, on passenger transport is the most important, because it will be experienced directly by european citizens, in their experience as passengers, and by railway workers, who are taking a leap into the unknown. we are going to be judged on this case by the pieces, and it is wrong to say that we will be able to revise this legislative package if it goes wrong. that's not true! we are committed for at least 20 years, the time for which all the stages of opening up to competition provided for in this package are being implemented. all this was well understood by european railway workers. they're drawing our attention because the legislature has done a bad job, and they're afraid for their future. what was done wrong? the first thing is that the european union has confused 'liberating' and 'liberalising' the railway. a very simple example: in 2006, freight was liberalised in europe. ten years later, traffic has dropped by 30 percent. we liberalized without liberating and we got the opposite effect of what we wanted. this example must therefore be borne in mind when passenger transport is opened up to competition. the risks to passenger transport are twofold: first, the risk of deterioration of public transport. the public service networks will be opened from 2023 and the operator will be selected by public procurement. there is no doubt that competition will be based on price and not on quality or high level of service. we must expect less safety on board, less dessert on the less profitable segments, because the text gives no guarantees on these aspects. the solution is simple: it was necessary to impose specifications with the most comprehensive possible european mandatory public service criteria, and that was removed from the text. we cannot vote on this text in these conditions. another worrying example is social pricing. other operators will not be obliged to offer social tariffs. what does that mean? no more low prices for students, the unemployed, the disabled or the elderly. it is at the very heart of public service and our european solidarity system. finally, for workers, what is happening is serious: a railway worker has no guarantee that in the event of a change of operator, his job on the network, which he is accustomed to serving, will be preserved. we are creating a job that is precarious and can be outsourced, with precariousness that will return with every contract. what do we want to show the citizens? the european union protecting them or making them insecure? so i tell you, the group of environmentalists here on wednesday will vote against this text because it contains principles of social breakdown and breakdown of public service. we will stand with the workers tomorrow in front of our european parliament, hoping that the other political groups, which make up the majority here, will come to their senses and resume discussions. the rapporteur. mr president, this regulation on deep-sea fishing is a highly symbolic regulation, which has been the subject of much discussion. you may sometimes wonder why, and yet the answers are there. firstly, because we are at the heart of the question of sustainable development, that is to say at the heart of the famous triangle which should be equilateral, defined in rio, between environment, economy and social. the fisheries sector is an economic activity which, in addition to the social function of its jobs, also has a social function in terms of food and, of course, a strong environmental impact. but beyond that, there is a great concern among our fellow citizens about what we will do with our oceans. since 2012, when the barroso commission proposed a ban on deep-sea fishing, we have been able to say: 'at least i was sure of it' 'that we could make this sustainable development work, which is often just a slogan, the certainty that a compromise was possible' 'not necessarily a compromise between the political groups, that is always possible, or almost so' but a compromise on the big issues, namely, precisely, the vulnerable seabed to be protected, the species to be protected, but also economic activity and its jobs and the food function. i must say that there was a lot of noise, a lot of anger, a lot of insults, death threats against me, incredible pressure, but we worked in the european parliament and in the council and we got an agreement which - i believe at any rate - meets our priorities and all these objectives. what are the results? first, the maintenance of the business. it's not nothing, it was still 760 ships. secondly, the freezing of the footprint, that is to say the definition of an area where we can continue to fish in deep waters, but which is limited to the one that was in force between 2009 and 2011. a bathymetric limit that will prohibit fishing below a half mile. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a regulation on the control of fishing activities by vessels flying its flag. scientific monitoring of fishing activities is quite exceptional, with 20 per cent of this activity to be covered by scientific observers. many impact studies and catch records, including non-target species. we certainly didn't choose the easy way out. it would have been much easier to do what the barroso commission had proposed, namely to prohibit everything, or even simpler, just as simple, to allow everything. legally, it would have been quite easy. that is why this regulation is so difficult and technical, because we have tried to bring all these requirements and issues together. this is also why it took the council two years to agree, and why it was hampered by many contradictions. this is also why we have had two presidencies of the council and in this connection i would like to thank the luxembourg presidency, which initiated this work, and the dutch presidency, which concluded it, and which accompanied us for nine months - mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome the adoption of this report, which is the culmination of four years of hard negotiations on deep-sea fishing in the european union. good for the reporter. starting from a radical proposal, the european parliament and the council have succeeded in drawing a clear and balanced line for deep-sea fisheries. we have had the difficult task of finding a compromise between our environmental ambitions to safeguard very slow-maturing species and the preservation of vulnerable ecosystems, and the safeguarding of regulated targeted and by-catch fisheries that are necessary for some of our european regions. this agreement will enable the collection of data essential to the knowledge of the seabed and of species still too little known, thanks to the presence of observers on board vessels. in addition, fishing vessels are only allowed to fish within the historical fishing footprint. when they encounter vulnerable marine ecosystems between 0 and 400 metres deep, they must now move away from them by a minimum of 5 nautical miles and report them to the national authorities. these areas will then be closed to fishing. i am glad that by-catch is allowed up to 11.5 tonnes per year, but that it is supervised and controlled. we have reached a balanced agreement that respects the marine environment and enhances the sustainability of fisheries, based on an awareness of the vulnerability of european and global seabeds. we have sought and obtained an agreement which is economically and ecologically sustainable and profoundly european. thank you, emilie, for everything you've helped me do in this house since 2009.

in writing. ‒ the subject of this report is deep-sea fishing in the north-east atlantic, which is mainly carried out by traditional coastal fleets (portugal) and large nomadic trawlers (france, spain). it is practised in union and international waters governed by agreements within the north-east atlantic fisheries commission (neafc). measures taken so far have not solved the problem of overfishing, due to the high vulnerability of these stocks. some of them can no longer withstand the pressure of fishing and their replenishment may prove very long or even impossible. bottom trawling damages vulnerable and irreplaceable marine ecosystems and trawl fishing for deep-sea species leads to high levels of bycatch. the new regulation provides for stricter regulations: a ban on trawling below 800 metres, a freezing of the footprint (obligation for vessels to fish only in areas already exploited between 2009 and 2011), increased on-board controls and penalties and greater transparency of the activity. i voted in favour of this regulation and against the amendment rejecting it.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this balanced report which preserves both the marine environment and deep-sea species, but also makes it possible to enhance the sustainability of fisheries. we have sought and obtained an agreement which is economically and ecologically sustainable and profoundly european. i am also pleased that by-catch is allowed up to 11.5 tonnes per year, but is supervised and controlled. now, deep-sea fishing is prohibited beyond 800 metres and vessels must avoid any vulnerable marine ecosystems between 0 and 400 metres. the presence of observers on board vessels allows the collection of data useful for the knowledge of species with very slow maturation. the implementation of this text will reduce the impact of this fishery on the seabed, while preserving a sustainable fishing activity necessary for our european market and jobs in coastal areas.
in writing. ‒ this legislative report proposes to establish specific conditions for fishing for deep-sea stocks in international waters of the north-east atlantic. the aim of this text is to ensure better management of fish stocks in this region, whose replenishment rate is particularly vulnerable to overexploitation. as such, it prohibits bottom trawling at a depth of more than 800 metres. at the same time, although deep-sea fisheries account for only around 1% of landings from the atlantic, many fishermen depend on this type of fishery to maintain their activity. i have supported this report because i believe that a balance has been struck in favour of the positions defended by my group.
in writing. i have approved the regulation establishing specific conditions for fishing for deep-sea stocks in the north-east atlantic and provisions for fishing in international waters of the north-east atlantic. deep-sea fishing, if unregulated, represents a considerable risk to the sustainable management of fish stocks. that is why we have adopted this regulation, which controls deep-sea fishing by making it subject to authorisation, prohibiting fishing at depths of more than 800 metres, delimiting the areas in which it can be carried out and imposing an increased presence of scientific observers on board vessels.
in writing. ‒ deep water is the largest ecosystem on the planet, but also one of the most sensitive. deep-sea trawling is a fishing method that destroys the deep sea. equipped with metal plates, the nets plough the seabed, crushing and damaging ecosystems that take several thousand years to rebuild. to combat this scourge, the eu has just approved a total ban on fishing below 800 metres in european waters. this is a world first. it is vital for the balance of the seas and for the balance of fisheries itself, in particular for small-scale, artisanal and coastal fishing, to allow these resources to be renewed. these are common goods and must be protected. so this decision is excellent news.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report and against the amendment to reject it. deep-sea fishing is carried out in eu and international waters governed by agreements within the north-east atlantic fisheries commission (neafc). in the european union, this fishery has been regulated since 2003. these regulations, which often include technical measures such as the ban on gillnets, have not solved the problem of overfishing. in addition, bottom trawling damages ecosystems, with 20 to 40% of catches being by accident. the new proposal for regulation is therefore more stringent. it provides, in particular, for a ban on trawling below 800 metres and for increased on-board checks and penalties. initially in favour of deep-sea fishing because of the jobs involved, the front national notes the gradual withdrawal of the only french company active in this sector of activity. we no longer have any reason to support this practice, which causes certain environmental problems.
in writing. ‒ for the report and against the rejection amendment: the current regulation provides for restrictive technical measures against certain fishing gear (ban on gillnets) and prohibits deep-sea fishing in certain areas. but these restrictions are not enough to guarantee sustainable fishing and protect these particularly fragile ecosystems.
in writing. ‒ i support this report, which is a satisfactory compromise between a total ban on deep-sea fishing and the protection of marine ecosystems. the damage caused by trawlers can be irreplaceable for both the environment and stocks because of the high rate of bycatch. nevertheless, the restrictions prescribed by the current regulations seem to be able to guarantee effective protection. the expertise of scientific observers will help to determine with certainty the potential for a sustainable level of fishing. i voted against the council's position.

in writing. ‒ following the adoption of parliament's position at first reading in plenary on 10 december 2013, trilogue negotiations were launched to reach an agreement in july 2016. trawl fishing in deep water is prohibited from 800 m and from 400 m for the areas called 'vulnerable marine environment'. in addition, the fishing footprint will be frozen and limited to areas where targeted fishing took place between 2009 and 2011. finally, parliament introduced new transparency rules, including the obligation to inform the public about european vessels targeting deep-sea species and to declare all catches (fish and vulnerable ecosystems). i wanted more and better. the negotiated outcome limits predation on the marine ecosystem while contributing to the sustainability of the fisheries sector. i am voting for this text.

in writing. ‒ as rapporteur, i was responsible for negotiating with the council the report on deep-sea fishing submitted to parliament, and i am pleased that it was adopted by a very large majority, with 634 votes in favour and 38 against. this vote is a reward for hard work and eight months of negotiations with the board. the agreement provides for a 'freezing of the footprint', i.e. the obligation for this fishery to be limited geographically to the areas already exploited between 2009 and 2011. it also provides for a ban on trawling below 800 metres. it shall strengthen controls and sanctions for infringers; it promotes better environmental knowledge through the collection of data on ships and the publication of studies on the impact on resources and ecosystems. this monitoring should allow the regulation to be adjusted to environmental realities. in 2012, a majority of meps rejected the commission's proposal to ban deep-sea fishing. we have worked with the council to develop regulations which take account of both environmental requirements and socioeconomic issues. this balance is the key to sustainable development.

in writing. ‒ protecting vulnerable marine ecosystems is fundamental to the future of our planet. deep-sea species are particularly threatened by intensive fishing activities. the european union has agreed on new delimitations of fishing zones in the north-east atlantic, which are set at 800 metres deep. the restrictions apply below 400 metres where endangered species live. ships found to be in breach of the legislation will have to suspend their activities and move away from the area in question with at least five thousand seamen. this limit applies to all vessels with a deep-sea fishing stock of at least 8%. the european parliament introduced new transparency rules, including the obligation to publish the names of vessels fishing in deep-sea waters and the obligation to declare all catches. member states will have to provide information on sites containing species at risk. finally, the commission will evaluate the data annually and adjust the fishing areas authorised accordingly. the european union also regulates deep-sea fishing and prohibits trawling. i voted for it, of course.
